A control failing its sweep: the failing interval = the smallest run of adjacent steps whose checks fail, widened by one step each side; (1) the control's expansion row (§7.7) is replaced over that interval by a smoothstep between the row's values at the interval's ends — a table change with provenance "sweep fallback" and a declared shift (§6.4) — and the sweep re-runs; (2) if still failing, it is declared discrete: the registry's continuity class becomes discrete with the levels at which the metric's mean is stable (steps between failing intervals, each represented by its median step), the basic and advanced panels show it stepped, and the report and release notes list it; the population control is continuous by construction (§10.2's prefix-stable roster) and checked the same way; its work-limit side is §5.1 (5)'s flat F-WORK rate.

"Surprise me" and the size / water controls preview six candidate towns as the towns' own S0-S4 runs (site, water, backbone at city LOD from those stages' display list in §8.5's distinct preview style) under the same deterministic work limits as a full generation (§5.1), so a proxy is bit-identical to the first stages of the town it previews; choosing one continues that recipe from its committed S4 state and asserts the S4 digest equals the proxy's; budgets on reference hardware (§12): all six within 1 s at TOWN (O16 (e)); at CITY and METROPOLIS progressively — the first within 300 ms, each within 250 ms at CITY and 500 ms at METROPOLIS.
Proxy budgets: six proxies within 1 s at TOWN; first within 300 ms, each within 250 ms at CITY and 500 ms at METROPOLIS.

The front door is one action; the basic panel holds ≤ 12 controls — seed (with the "Surprise me" dice as its button), size rung, water setting and side, walls, castle, gates, features (one checkbox strip — plaza, temple, shanty town, farms, greens: MFCG's first-level toggles, counted as one), planned ↔ organic, wealth level, greenery, style preset, labels; a feature left at auto is drawn as §4.2 S0 states and reported (§5.4); everything else behind an advanced panel; 100 % of parameters documented (registry test); new templates and presets are data, not code; release notes name known defects; the toolkit's T1 intend is this panel, not a thirteenth control: its site cards are the water setting and side (each card carrying a form of the forms catalogue and an era-and-region preset), its size the size rung, its two sliders the wealth level and the walls (item 101 (g)), its style the style preset — the toolkit adds no basic control, every slider keeps its sweep (J-A101.77).
Basic panel ≤ 12 controls.

The day and night switch (light), the sun's mode and height (sunMode, sunHeight) and the underground hand lantern (handLantern) are per-viewer view keys (§2.9) set from the view bar beside the layer toggles: view controls with no model effect, never logged, in no digest, outside the basic panel's count; each has its registry row (label, range, anchor, continuity class — sunHeight continuous, the others discrete), default §8.4's; the pointer moving the cursor sun is a transient input, never a key (§6.2).
LOCALITY CLASS (local / re-derive from Sk), CONTINUITY CLASS (continuous / discrete), CONSUMING STAGE, CONTROL REGISTRY, BASIC PANEL / ADVANCED PANEL, VIEW KEY vs model feature.

EFFECTIVE SCOPE: the coarsest faces covering an edit's scope at its level (union of chained operators' scopes; the touched set for a designation change, dossier event, positive placement or relocation), shown before commit and stored resolved as EditScope. Names used: "effective scope", "effective-scope faces", "resolved EditScope". Hazard: "scope" also names the invariant scopes of §5.3 and the batch scope of §5.1 (5).

SEAM EXCEPTION: the neighbour-side vertices, corridor records, half-corridor strips, junction wedges, rings through those vertices and Seam records a district-scoped re-derivation may touch outside its scope; empty for the underground and island arenas. Names used: "the seam exception".

TREE SCOPING: discarding every unprotected finer entity under the effective scope and re-running the refinement stages there ("sound by over-invalidation"; the primary mechanism). Names used: "tree scoping", "tree scope".
EDIT FATE: kept / carried / orphaned / discarded (plus the listing "kept (declared)"); the list is the fate report. Names used: "fate", "fate report", "fate list", "edit-fate report", "fates".

NAMED ACTIONS: Regenerate (keep settings), New random, Adjust, Re-derive from stage k (Sk), Same kind new seed (Enter's successor), Surprise me; a designation change is neither a regeneration nor a re-roll. Names used: "Regenerate (keep settings)", "faithful Regenerate", "New random", "reroll", "Re-derive from Sk", "Enter".

PROTECTION CLASSES: locked (entity or attribute paths), pinned, edited (implicit pin), assigned (held within drift bounds), dossier-backed (existence held), positively placed (placeAt pin), declared (held by its declaring event), a closure's created piece. Names used: "protected entity", "fixed input", "held", "kept".
DELIVERY TIER: a requested feature is delivered full (tier <= 3), degraded (tiers 4-5) or omitted (tier 6). Names used: "full", "degraded", "omitted", "delivery tier".

WORK LIMIT: an output-changing limit stated as an operation count law over the batch scope (WorkLimitLaw), never a time limit; its hit is E_WORK_LIMIT handled as F-WORK. Names used: "work limit", "operation count", "work-limit coefficients", "work_cut", "workLimitHits". Hazard: "work" also names item 67's Works records.

DERIVED-COMPLETE DIGEST: the digest of every district's lazily derived stages computed in random orders and pool sizes, required identical (the laziness contract's test). Names used: "derived-complete digest".

MODEL DIGEST vs RECORDS DIGEST: the Merkle root over the eager model versus the second Merkle tree over persisted derivation and naming records (recordsDigest); goldens, locality checks and bridge convergence read the model digest alone; replay = session and truncation identity compare both.

INDEPENDENCE: the undo precondition that every later live event's touched set and effective-scope faces are disjoint from the target's (dilated one ring), extended to input-layer dependence (tables, adjust, town-wide naming reroll). Names used: "independence check", "dependent events".

TRUNCATION: dropping an immediately undone pair from an unshared document's log while holding the target on the redo stack; truncation identity is its test. Names used: "truncation", "truncated log", "truncation identity".

SESSION (authoring): an authoring identity per document and author holding undo and redo stacks, never read by the fold. Hazard: "session" also means the running app session (§6.5 (9) session-history independence: maps generated earlier in that session) and the live state compared by "replay = session".

CHECKPOINT: a copy-on-write snapshot taken when accumulated replay cost passes 80 ms, before every epoch, rebase and upgrade, and at h0 for an off-edit-path load recomputation. Names used: "checkpoint", "h0".

ORPHAN: an edit or override left without a target (no successor, a vanished table row, an unmapped entity), kept in the log and listed in the orphan table, never silently re-bound. Names used: "orphan", "orphaned", "orphan table".

REBASE / FROZEN VIEW / RETENTION WINDOW: a rebase makes a state the document's base (reasons keptSnapshot, drawnConstraintsRebuilt, frozenImport); a document outside the N-1/N-2 window opens as a frozen view. Names used: "rebase", "rebased base", "kept snapshot", "frozen view", "frozenImport", "the window", "N-1, N-2".

PARITY PRESET / EXTENSION CELL: the MFCG and FTG presets zero every extension cell's chance or weight and switch its option off, resolving a cell by its own presets entry first. Hazard: "preset" also names the style preset (§7.8), the era-and-region preset (§7.7) and editPreset (§7.1).

SLICE / NAMING SLICE: the recorded unit of table dependence (row, weights, bracket, thresholds, match); a naming slice is one field of a culture or ancestry row. Names used: "slice", "naming slice", "slice kinds", "slice hash".

DERIVATION TABLE (rows DR1-DR25): the index of map-fact families with their dossier inputs, rule home, chance concern and bar. Hazard: distinct from the derivation RECORD (§2.8) and the derivation UNIT (§6.3).

RECEIPT TABLE (rows F1-F22): per change kind, the receipt fields in precedence order and the response. Hazard: the F-row ids (F1 ... F22) sit beside the failure-class ids (F-NUM, F-CUT ...) in the same section family.

BINDING KEY / KEY LAW / DOSSIER BINDING / CARRIED FACTS: the dossier-side identity of an element (settlement:, inst:cat:, inst:uid:, inst:name:, power:, npc:, cond:, res:, quarter:, government) bound to a map address in Document.dossier; carried facts are the "previous dossier" the port diffs against.
CHANGE ENVELOPE: the DossierChange a dossier change carries on every event it generates (changeId, source, week, cause, element, op, reason, receipts).
NAMING CLAIM / NAMED-FEATURE CLAIM: a quarter entering the map as a neighbourhood assignment that names and biases, never zones; a landmark string the roster demands as a feature-granularity claim.

REJECTION / LAPSE / POSITIVE PLACEMENT: a map "delete" of a dossier-backed element recorded as a site exclusion that lapses on growth, decline or a dossier event over its block; placeAt pins an element or designation to a plot. Names used: "rejection", "lapse", "lift", "positive placement".

DISRUPTION: the cost of a placement (moved uses, joins, subtracted parts, vacated plots) against a request kind's budget row; a dossier event over budget still lands and is reported. Names used: "disruption", "disruption budget", "disruption report", "over budget", "disruption set".
PRECEDENCE ORDER: lock > dossier existence > assignment > user-drawn geometry > rule tables > defaults — the one order for every meeting of protections and inputs.

CHANGED REACH / FOOTPRINT / KEPT WAY / SUCCESSOR SITE / DETOUR BOUND: the water operator's vocabulary — where new shores differ from old; the union of L1 cells an edit clears; a way re-routed through a deck (arterial, sole connection, or one that crossed on a deck); the new site nearest an old deck; re-routed length <= 1.4 x the old.

TOOLKIT LAYERS L0-L4: intent, ground and bones, programme, fabric, finish (the author may stop at any layer). HAZARD: the same labels L0-L4 name the arena refinement levels (§2.2) used in the same sections ("one L1 batch", "L0 batch", "fromLevel", §7.3).
FORM / FORMS CATALOGUE: a row { id, constraints, growthProgramme, signature } naming a settlement archetype; Intent.form names one.

LADDER (naming hazard): the failure ladder (§5), the size ladder (§1.1, "rung" TOWN/CITY/METROPOLIS), the interior ladder (§2.6, item 28 (f)), the survivors' ladder (§4.11, rungs 1-3 in §5.3's epoch rows) and the label rungs (F-LABEL, §9.4) all appear in this unit with "rung" for their steps (see DETERMINISM-0025).

SCOPE (naming hazard): invariant scope (batch-local ... CI-only), batch scope (the count a work-limit law reads), edit scope (EditScope) and effective scope are four meanings of one word in this unit.

"ITEM n" (naming hazard): "§7.7 item n" is the dossier contract's item; bare "item n" elsewhere is the owner's amendment item; inside §7.7 bare items 12-16 mean contract items while amendment items 12-16 exist with other meanings (see DIC-05).

All shape mathematics lives in one kernel library that never throws and never guesses: whole-cm coordinates, exact side-of-line tests, every new line snapped and checked, typed failure reasons instead of exceptions or garbage.
Every generation stage changes geometry only through transactions: a batch of changes accepted whole after its rules are checked, or rejected whole; this is what removes whole-map retries.
Lattice, snapping and attraction are BUILT in-house; degenerate inputs specified by §3.2 and §3.6.

Exact predicates: orient2d BUILT (exact in doubles under the range invariant §3.2 (1)); incircle ADOPTED from robust-predicates 3.0.3 (Unlicense; J-K36), licence confirmed against the public registry (docs/validation/redteam-improve.md §5.1), version pinned and re-checked by §17.4 licence checker on every upgrade; pre-decided fallback if a future version fails: in-house BigInt incircle (exact, slower). incircle is adaptive and never on the topology path; ties by §3.2 (3), orientation and areas by §3.2 (6).

Planar subdivision (the §2.2 record) is BUILT as the core asset: struct-of-arrays with allocation-free hot loops, because in the NG 1.2.2 profile creating points (385-561 k calls) and intersecting lines (147-213 k calls) dominate (G-R7). Its transactions §3.3, insertion and slivers §3.6, storage §3.9, invariants §3.10.

Polygon booleans, buffers, offsets, insets and bands are BUILT on the kernel arrangement (§3.7; J-K4). Clipper2 (BSL-1.0) and polygon-clipping (MIT) serve as CI oracles only, shipped only under §3.7 fallback.

Straight skeleton is BUILT (§3.8; J-K5, J-A21.31); none adopted: no permissive mature JS/TS skeleton meets §3.8 numeric contract; CGAL skeleton is GPL (rest LGPL), excluded by §17.4 permissive-only production closure (module licence the owner's, §17.3), and fails the stack and one-engine grounds (C++ is not the TypeScript kernel every host runs, D-4; no WASM kernel, §3.7; its doubles cannot be byte-identical to §3.8 validated construction).

OBB, convex hull and largest inscribed rectangle BUILT: monotone chain + rotating calipers; LIR sampled deterministically over four candidate axes: OBB long axis, frontage normal, +45 deg and -45 deg (G-R13).

GEO-7 degenerate contract for OBB/hull/LIR: fewer than 3 distinct points or a collinear hull returns E_DEGENERATE (detail collinear), never ok with a zero extent, so no caller divides by a zero minor axis; callers branch on the typed result.

Best-fit regular polygon regularFit BUILT (§3.4; J-A45.31): a ring of fewer than 3 vertices, of zero area, or whose first component vanishes (radius below 1 cm) returns E_DEGENERATE (detail fit); a clockwise ring is read in reverse; cosines, sines and angles through dmath (§6.5).

Delaunay/Voronoi ADOPTED: delaunator (ISC), d3-delaunay (ISC); duplicate points merged first; used only for site sampling, Lloyd relaxation, field seeds and medial axes, never as the street source (the S4 routing lattice is hexLattice, §3.4).

Poisson-disc/blue noise BUILT: Bridson with k = 50 candidates, all evaluated, each drawn in the §8.10 candidate annulus (poisson.annulus) about its active point, on a torus (wrap-around tile) - the sampler of MFCG build 12710731, VG 1.6.9, NG 1.2.2 and Dwellings itch 17195045 as their code reads (P14; k = 50 measured by _critic.md C2; G-P17); run at PRODUCT BUILD TIME to make the §8.10 stamp tiles; per-instance placement by §8.1 (2) and §8.10. Domain clipped to any polygon with holes; an empty domain returns empty.
A ragged wood edge comes from thinning the stamped points by the domain-warped density noise (§4.9), never from warping the Poisson sampler (COV-VG-WC3).

Noise (fBm, domain warp, ridged): simplex-noise (MIT) ADOPTED; seeding, fBm and warp BUILT; seeded from sub-streams (§6.1); octaves and lacunarity are table values (VG 5-octave field, _critic-vg-ng.md V7).

Curves BUILT: Chaikin, centripetal Catmull-Rom to cubic, pinned-vertex Laplacian, Visvalingam-Whyatt, circular fillets. Results re-enter through insertChain; smoothing committed geometry is a warp (§3.4, §3.6); Visvalingam-Whyatt is the topology-preserving simplify (§3.4); fillets are skipped when a leg is shorter than the chord.
Spatial index: flatbush (ISC) ADOPTED for static partitions plus a uniform grid per level (§3.3); rbush (MIT) only for the screen-space label collision index (§9).

Marching squares ADOPTED (d3-contour, ISC; §17 licence table); distance transform BUILT, linear time. VG 1.6.9 costliest terrain routine (a field pushing roads and highway entrance away from water) is not reproduced - the S4 lattice crossing penalty (§4.3) keeps roads off water; VG grid-staircase coastlines smoothed in two passes and resampled are replaced by contour extraction; contours are extracted per render tile, not in S1, and are never plat edges (§2.3, §8).

Path search BUILT: binary-heap A*/Dijkstra on rasters and on the subdivision graph; the 2017 A* and the MFCG 12710731 street search are FIFO searches with no heuristic, not reproduced (J-A53.31); failure returns E_NO_PATH with the closest reached point.
Triangulation (render, fields) ADOPTED: earcut (ISC); holes supported; degenerate triangles skipped and reported.
Deterministic math dmath BUILT (§6.5 (2); J-11); a division by a computed value goes through ratio() (§3.2 (8)).
RNG and hashing BUILT (§6.1).
Every kernel primitive returns a typed KernelResult and never throws for a geometric reason.
type KernelResult<T> = { ok: true; value: T; warnings: Warning[] } | { ok: false; code: KernelError; detail: string; partial?: T }.

type KernelError: the closed enumeration of 18 failure codes (E_OUT_OF_RANGE, E_DEGENERATE, E_LEVEL, E_LOCKED, E_KEPT, E_SCOPE, E_STRUCTURAL, E_NOT_TWO_CROSSINGS, E_HOLE_CONTACT, E_SELF_INTERSECT, E_BELOW_MIN_EDGE, E_BELOW_MIN_ANGLE, E_BELOW_MIN_AREA, E_BELOW_MIN_WIDTH, E_NON_CONVEX, E_NO_PATH, E_WORK_LIMIT, E_INVARIANT).
E_OUT_OF_RANGE: snap() given a non-finite value or |coordinate| >= 2^23 cm - a caller bug, reported with its stream key, never stored (§3.2 (7)).

E_DEGENERATE: ratio() with a vanishing denominator; OBB/hull of collinear or <3 distinct points; an empty or collapsed boolean, buffer or inset; a StretchRef whose ends are not two distinct vertices of one part of its chain (detail stretch); a transient arena seed or fixed ring breaking minEdge, clearance or simplicity, overlapping input rings, or a seed clip piece left with a hole (detail seed, fixed or overlap); a regular fit of <3 vertices, zero-area ring or vanishing first component (detail fit).

E_LEVEL: a batch wrote a level other than its own, added a row coarser than the edge or vertex it lands on, or - in a clear-region batch - met finer geometry inside its region away from its prepared contacts (§3.3).
E_LOCKED: the op would cut, move or delete geometry owned by a locked or pinned entity - returned to the dry run as a conflict (§7.1).
E_KEPT: an insertion or clear would cross, clear or come within attractCm of kept content (§3.3) - a stage-domain bug in generation, a conflict in an edit dry run.
E_SCOPE: a pool district overlay wrote outside its district scope, or two overlays touched one record (§3.3).
E_STRUCTURAL: a merge or removal would delete an edge carrying a structural role (§2.2 rule 7) or a transient arena fixed edge (§3.4).
E_NOT_TWO_CROSSINGS: splitFace contact semantics violated (§3.6).
E_HOLE_CONTACT: connectHole post-condition violated (§3.6).
E_SELF_INTERSECT: a ring whose role requires a simple polygon (a claim, a drawn boundary) crosses itself.
E_BELOW_MIN_EDGE: optional chains only; its two triggers are those of §3.6.
E_BELOW_MIN_ANGLE: optional chains only: a face corner below minFaceAngle (§3.6).
E_BELOW_MIN_AREA: a class floor (minimum area) declared by the caller was violated.
E_BELOW_MIN_WIDTH: a class floor (minimum width) declared by the caller was violated.
E_NON_CONVEX: the half-plane inset path was asked for a non-convex face (§3.7).
E_NO_PATH: path search found no path; returned with the closest reached point (§3.1 path search row).
E_WORK_LIMIT: an operation-count budget was exhausted - counted in operations, never measured by a clock (§3.3).
E_INVARIANT: a declared hard invariant failed at commit (§3.10).

type Warning = { code: W_ATTRACTED | W_STRETCH_SHARED | W_WEDGE_ROUTED | W_PLACED | W_PROMOTED | W_SNAP_PASSES | W_ACUTE_CORNER | W_SLIVER_RETYPED | W_STEINER | W_HEIGHT_CLAMPED | W_DOWNGRADE | W_CUT_SLID; count: number; at?: LatticePoint } - 12 warning codes, each with a count and an optional lattice point.
W_ATTRACTED: a new vertex was attracted onto existing geometry (§3.6).
W_STRETCH_SHARED: a stretch was shared between rows (§3.4/§3.6).
W_WEDGE_ROUTED: an acute wedge was routed (§3.6).
W_PLACED: §3.6 placement rule placed a point on an existing edge.
W_PROMOTED: a finer vertex was promoted (§2.2 rule 3) - prepared vertices and stretch ends included.
W_SNAP_PASSES: snap-rounding needed extra passes (§3.6).
W_ACUTE_CORNER: a soft minFaceAngle corner kept (§3.6/§3.10).
W_SLIVER_RETYPED: a sliver face was retyped (§3.6).
W_STEINER: Steiner points were added (§3.7 overlay or §3.6).
W_HEIGHT_CLAMPED: a height was clamped (§3.4/§3.9).
W_DOWNGRADE: an operation downgraded to a simpler shape (skeleton downgrades §3.8).
W_CUT_SLID: §4.6 step 8 (c) slid always-succeeding cut; count = the slide steps (J-Fredteam-1).
interface Frame { widthCm: Cm; heightCm: Cm; aspect: number (width/height, 0.5-2); marginShare: 0.3 (context margin per side) }.

(1) Integer world: all persisted geometry is integer cm; intermediate rational points (crossings, offsets, circumcentres, skeleton nodes) are computed in doubles and immediately placed on the lattice - by the §3.6 placement rule for points on existing edges, by nearest-point rounding otherwise.

(1) Range invariant: |x|, |y| < 2^23 cm (83.9 km), enforced by snap (7); then every coordinate difference < 2^24, every orient2d term < 2^48, the determinant < 2^49, so the sign of orient2d is exact in ordinary doubles. Every exactness argument rests on this invariant, never on the frame table, so a rescaled frame (§13.7 O14 (e)) cannot break one.

(1) Headroom check: the largest arena is METROPOLIS at the population cap 120 000 (§12.2: 153.6 km²) at aspect 2 = 17.53 km x 8.76 km plus 30 % margin each side, so |x| <= 0.8 x 17.53 km = about 1 402 000 cm = about 2^20.4, leaving about 6x headroom; about 9x at the METROPOLIS target (11.31 km x 5.66 km at aspect 2, |x| <= 905 097 cm = about 2^19.8).
owner_raw: kernel (population cap and 153.6 km² owned by §12.2 / §1.1)
restates_note: §12.2 cap figure 153.6 km² and population cap 120 000

statement: (2) Tolerances are world lengths, never parameter-space (the OS DELTA = 1e-6 on line parameters is the anti-pattern).
(2) minEdge = 25 cm: the minimum edge length on the lattice (named minEdgeCm in §2.2 LatticeSpec).

(2) attractCm = 26 cm = minEdge + 1 cm of lattice slack, so a vertex split onto an edge lies at least attractCm - 0.71 cm = 25.29 cm from both of the edge endpoints; a vertex whose exact foot lies within attractCm of an endpoint moves onto that endpoint instead (§3.6 step 2).
(2) minFaceAngle = 5 deg (500 centidegrees); hard or soft by chain class (§3.10). Named minFaceAngleCdeg in §2.2 LatticeSpec.

(2) Class floors come from the stage tables: minPlotWidth = 2.5 m, minInteriorAnglePlot = 12 deg (FTG sheared quads at p95 22.9 deg corner deviation stay legal - invariants police validity, not regularity), minCorridor per class.
(2) Face-size floors are a minimum width and a minimum area; angle floors are angles; none of them is minEdge.

(2) GEO-35 one minimum-edge rule for every writer: insertChain, booleans, buffers, offsets, smoothing and warp create or move edges only through §3.6 insertion semantics or move validation, and §3.10 checks the same minEdge on new AND moved edges.
(2) There is no weld tolerance: coincidence is lattice-point equality, proximity is attraction (§3.6; J-K2).

(3) No float comparisons for topology: equality is index equality; "same place" is a lattice test; collinear and cocircular ties are broken deterministically on lattice positions, never on slot ids; no predicate compares a float with == 0; any float that decides a topology operation is first quantised to integer cm or to a 16-bit binary angle.

(3) A distance comparison against attractCm or minEdge on a computed point (an exact foot, a crossing) uses + - x / sqrt only, so every IEEE engine gives the same answer; a borderline case may fall either way without breaking any bound, because the 1 cm between attractCm and minEdge exceeds the 0.71 cm of any single rounding.

(4) Cross-platform reproducibility is §6.5 policy (integer-derived random floats §6.1; nightly cross-platform golden run §13.3); the kernel part is integer geometry, exact predicates, one geometry engine on every host (§3.7) and a deterministic op order in every batch (§3.3).
(5) Angles and directions are unit vectors in doubles derived from integer endpoints; growth headings are stored as centidegrees.

(6) area2(ring) (GEO-32; J-K13) returns twice the signed area as an exact integer for every ring snap can produce: each shoelace term x_i*y_(i+1) - x_(i+1)*y_i on coordinates relative to the ring bounding-box minimum corner (in [0, 2^24)), each product an exact double < 2^48; summed in a double partial flushed into a BigInt accumulator whenever its magnitude reaches 2^52 (one comparison per term), so every partial < 2^52 + 2^48 < 2^53 and every addition exact. Faces at the frame table sizes never reach the flush (terms < 2^43). Returned as an exact double because a simple ring twice-area < 2^49 (every face ring simple, §3.10).
(6) area2Big(ring) returns the BigInt twice-area of a self-crossing ring - only a boolean operand before its overlay can be one.
(6) Receipt: three star rings of radius 2^23 - 2 whose terms all share one sign are exact (docs/validation/bench/fixall_kernel_r2_attract.out section E).

(6) Ring orientation is orient2d at the ring lowest-leftmost vertex; no orientation, sliver or degeneracy decision reads the sign of a float sum; area statistics in m² are derived from the exact integer.

(7) GEO-7 the one door: snap(x, y) is the only way a number becomes an arena coordinate; in EVERY build (not only debug) it rejects !(Math.abs(v) < 2**23), one comparison per coordinate that also catches NaN and +-Infinity, with E_OUT_OF_RANGE; so NaN, +-Infinity and values past 2^31 never reach an Int32Array (which would store them silently as 0, 0 and a wrapped value - executed in GEO-7), and the null-rect crash class cannot return as a vertex at the world origin. Height and depth rasters have their own check (§2.3).

(8) Checked ratios: in model packages a division by a computed value goes through ratio(num, den, kind), which returns E_DEGENERATE when |den| is below the quantity floor (length 1 cm, area 1 cm², angle 1 centidegree, count 1); a lint rule flags every other division whose divisor is not a non-zero literal.
(8) Lint rule: flags every division in model packages whose divisor is not a non-zero literal (must use ratio()).

(9) Frames are rectangles (COV-VG-VN-156): a rung declares its frame AREA at its target population, A_target = frameAreaKm2AtTarget (§1.1: TOWN 4 km², CITY 25 km², METROPOLIS 64 km² = squares of 2, 5 and 8 km at the default aspect), scaled within the band by the requested population A = A_target * population / target (the side with its square root; item 9; cap figures §12.2); aspect in [0.5, 2] (default 1) gives width = sqrt(A * aspect), height = sqrt(A / aspect), centred on (0, 0) with +y north; the arena spans the frame plus marginShare on every side; every raster cols x rows follows width x height.
owner_raw: kernel (rung areas owned by §1.1 ladder table)
restates_note: §1.1 rung frame areas (TOWN 4, CITY 25, METROPOLIS 64 km²)

statement: (9) The range bound of (1) is taken at the population cap and the extreme aspect, so a non-square town (village product, river and coast towns) needs no other change.
(9) The arena outer ring and the frame rectangle are the margin and border chains of §2.2 rule 1.

(9) Frame growth at an epoch (item 81 (b); J-A81.31): a frame only grows, and only where §4.11 grows it at an epoch; the new frame is the (9) rule at the epoch population target, taken at most at the cap (as §1.1 clamps a request), at the frame own aspect, centred on (0, 0), so it encloses its predecessor; the range bound holds for every grown coordinate. The growth runs as §3.3 declared sequence of single-level batches sharing one clear region, each with rederivesFrom S1.
Defined term LAPSING STRETCH: a stretch of the old margin ring or of the old border rectangle that carries no other row of its chain level or a coarser one.
Defined term REGION (of a frame growth): the union of the L1 faces beside a lapsing stretch and those the new frame rectangle will cross - whole L1 faces, as a carve footprint is (§3.3).

Frame growth (a) Clearing (L1): one L1 batch removes the content finer than L1 of every face of the region (§3.3 rule 1); a locked or pinned owner returns as a conflict (F-EDIT, §5.2), so no deletion of the committed growth joins two faces finer than L1 and its new rectangle crosses none.

Frame growth (b) The margin (L0): one L0 batch inserts the new outer ring as the margin chain, then S1 water faces in the band between old and new ring (§4.11), then strips the old ring margin rows by removeEdges on two StretchRefs that together cover it (§3.4). A stretch left with no row is deleted, joining the faces either side (land with land, water with water, each cleared L1 face beside it with the ring one); a stretch that keeps a row keeps its edge, re-levelled by §2.2 rule 3 (a) (as where S1 lays a shore along it). Plat.frame takes the new frame as this batch commits.

Frame growth (c) The border (L1): one L1 batch inserts the new frame rectangle as the border chain by §3.6 insertion (a way it crosses sharing the crossing vertex) and strips the old rectangle border rows alike; a stretch that also carries another L1 row - the settlement perimeter or a reservation boundary running along the frame (§2.2 rule 1) - stays.

Frame growth: a vertex of an old chain that keeps a row or another edge stays (a through-road end on the old ring is an antenna end until §4.11 continues its way); every other vertex dissolves or stays by §2.2 rule 3.

Frame growth of underground parts: every underground part (its outer ring the frame with its margin - the sewer II.7.2, each further part §2.2 rule 1) grows by (a) and (b) on its own key, the margin rows of its own record (§2.2 rule 1) instead of the Terrain ones, with no water and no border.
owner_raw: kernel (parts owned by §2.2 / II.7 / V04 underground)

statement: Frame growth of rasters: each §2.3 raster extends by whole cells on each side until it covers the grown arena, keeping its cellCm and cell alignment, so every old cell keeps its place and every stored height its value; S1 fills the new cells; the hydro fields (flow direction, flat rank, accumulation) are recomputed over the grown grid by the §2.3 mechanism (an old edge cell gains neighbours and the ring may drain inward), every river traced course inside the old arena unchanged.

Frame growth: what changes is the region faces, the faces beside a deleted stretch and the ring new faces, at each level that sees them - §4.11 stages continue the ways and re-derive them; every other face keeps its ring, owner and nested faces (re-parented where its parent was joined, §3.3).

Frame growth draws no random stream in the kernel part, so a replay of the log re-grows the frame byte for byte; where §7.4 allows an epoch undo, its undo record restores the old frame and what the three batches removed.

Pre-decided fallback: if M4 memory measurement of the extreme growth - a TOWN grown in one epoch to the cap, whose kept 5 m heights over the cap arena are about 15.7 M cells (about 63 MB; a METROPOLIS made at the cap holds about 3.9 M) - exceeds the §12.8 METROPOLIS line, a growth that changes the rung re-grids each raster at the new rung cellCm (heights by the sampler bilinear read of the old grid, flow fields recomputed, every standing entity keeping its stored baseCm), and the generation report (§5.4) names the re-grid.
owner_raw: kernel (budget owned by §12.8; milestone M4 by §16)

statement: interface KernelTx { key: ArenaKey (a PlatKey or a transient arena TransientKey, §3.4); level: Level; ops: KernelOp[] (declared form only: independent ops, applied in canonical order); expect: Invariant[]; onFail: reject | repair | downgrade; batch: BatchScope; stage: StageId (the stage whose code issues the batch); rederivesFrom: StageId (earliest stage the batch re-derives: = stage in generation; the start of the edit re-derivation for an edit (§7.3); the first stage of §4.1 order for a warp or smoothing batch, which keeps nothing (§3.6; J-K33)); clearRegion?: Ring[] (coarse batch into finished fabric and its preparation batches); prepared?: VertexRef[] (with clearRegion: vertices earlier batches of the same edit or stage placed for this batch contacts with finer geometry, the only finer vertices it may meet, §3.6 candidate (c)); workLimit: number (operations, from the stage declaration §4.1, §14) }.

type BatchScope = { kind: stage; stage } | { kind: district; id } | { kind: block; id } | { kind: edit; edit: EditId } | { kind: entity; id } (a transient arena batches: the entity whose derivation opened it).

interface CommitRecord (returned by every commit; kernel-internal slots, never persisted): version; key; level; faces per level >= batch level {created, changed, removed} (the dirty set); edgesAdded; edgesRemoved; steinerAdded; steinerDissolved; moved: VertexId[] (vertices a warp or smoothing moved, Steiner re-seats included - their incident edges are §3.10 moved edges, GEO-35); promoted: VertexId[] (finer vertices whose birth level the batch lowered, §2.2 rule 3 - contacts, prepared vertices, stretch ends; the edit undo record keeps their lattice points, former levels and flags and the anchor contact names promotion stripped, §7.4); demoted: { vertices; edges (one half-edge per pair) } (birth levels raised; undo keeps former levels); unflagged: VertexId[] (split flag or kernel pin cleared other than by moving - prepared contact or stretch end promotion, a broken run, a pin released by §2.2 rule 3 (b), an unmoved vertex beside which a move displaced its run; undo restores flags); owners: Id[]; roles: RoleKey[] ((role, entity, ordinal) keys whose chains changed); warnings; work.
Batch granularity: a transaction batch is one growth stage, one district infill, one block plot subdivision or one edit; every insertion is part of a batch.

Transient arena batches use this protocol with level 0 (its one level); batch { kind: entity } naming the entity whose derivation opened it; stage and rederivesFrom both the stage id under which the opening rung draws its streams (§6.1), so no face on it is kept content; no clearRegion or prepared.

Batch execution: the kernel applies the ops to a scratch overlay, serves every query inside the batch from the level dynamic grid plus the static partitions, validates the batch-local invariants on the touched faces and their one-ring (§3.10), and commits or rejects atomically. Local repair (§5) runs inside the transaction on the overlay; for a batch an edit dry run has already validated, see §5.3.

One level per transaction: a batch creates vertices, edges, owners and roles of its own level only, plus the Steiner vertices, promotions and demotions of §2.2 rule 3; it may clear finer content inside its faces (clearFiner, subject to kept content); a warp batch moves vertices of every level >= its own (§3.6); anything else is E_LEVEL. A lane a finer stage would add to a coarser level is a separate coarser transaction (§4.7); a stage writing two levels (S3: carvings L0, reservations L1) issues one transaction per level in §4.1 batch-table order.

Kept content (J-K14): every face records the rank of the stage whose batch created it (LevelFaces.stage, §2.2; rank = the stage position in §4.1 topological order, fixed per generator version). A batch clears finer content inside its faces only where that content stage rank >= that of rederivesFrom; finer faces an earlier stage made are KEPT - neither cleared nor re-owned - and their edges and vertices are obstacles: an op crossing a kept edge, splitting a kept face or bringing new geometry within attractCm of it returns E_KEPT, except where §3.6 candidate (b) attracts onto and promotes a finer vertex on a route the chain ends on or joins.

E_KEPT governs insertion and clearing only; a move keeps nothing (§3.6). The re-walk re-parents each kept face into the new face containing it (a kept face never straddles a new edge because crossing it is refused), so nesting holds.

In generation E_KEPT cannot arise on a correct pipeline because the stage order builds no finer face before a coarser stage could meet it (wall band parts §4.7 S10 (0), §4.8; hinterland L3 content §4.9); the rule turns a wrong stage domain into a typed failure caught by the stage property tests (§13.2). In an edit it returns to the dry run as a conflict (§7.1). Wall and margin bands rebuilt in a re-derivation scope never write the other side: §7.3 item 2. clearFiner never removes kept content and never reports it as a conflict; only locked or pinned content is a conflict (§2.2 rule 6).

A batch faces are the faces it names or creates. A same-level split of an edge those faces share with outside faces - the neighbour step kerb split beside finished plots and footprints (II.1 (3)) - adds that vertex to the outside faces rings; they are not the batch kept content, neither cleared nor re-owned, and each ring equals its prior ring with the vertex removed (the seam exception, §4.6 step 7, §7.3 item 1).

Clear regions and prepared contacts (LC-7; J-I10, J-I12, J-I13, J-K24): a coarse batch inserted into finished fabric - §4.11 carve of a canal, moat or basin, §4.4 outer moat, S1 water operator re-carving a reach (§7.3 (b)), an epoch frame growth (§3.2 (9)) - runs as a declared sequence of single-level batches sharing one CLEAR REGION (KernelTx.clearRegion), because under the plain rule one canal would clear the town (an L0 face is a whole land component).

Defined term FOOTPRINT (of an edit, the clear region): computed by the operator in its dry run (§4.11 carve and outer moat; §7.3 (b) 2-4 re-carved reach; for frame growth the whole L1 faces §3.2 (9) names instead): its new chains buffered (buffer, §3.7) by attractCm plus the clearance of the chain class (a channel: its bank setback), UNITED with every L1 cell the edit way rule touches - cells that buffer meets, cells bordering a stretch the edit removes or prunes or a kept way replaced stretch, cells a re-routed way crosses, and where the edit re-traces a wall run the cells bordering the old run or the strip-line stretches it removes and the cells the re-traced run new strips will take. The footprint is exactly the union of those cells, since the buffer lies inside the cells it meets.

Clear region rule 1 Clearing: clearFiner in a batch declaring a clear region removes each finer face whose interior meets the region - whole, never part - with the partition edges and vertices no remaining face uses, nothing else; locked and pinned owners return as conflicts; every finer face not meeting the region is kept content whatever its stage rank. Structural finer edges inside the region (ways, walls, setback and glacis lines, deck spans) are kept unless a preceding batch of the same edit removed them: clearFiner removes partition content only, and preparation (rule 2) re-lays or cuts every structural edge the coarse chain would meet (§4.11 batch (1), §7.3 (b) 3). The coarse batch itself clears nothing; it only splits the finer faces meeting the region (rule 3).

Clear region rule 2 Preparation: one or more finer-level batches, issued first in the same edit or stage, clear the region (rule 1) and place EVERY point where the coarse chain will meet finer geometry as a vertex named by role (§2.2 rule 7): (i) on each way kept across the new water, a deck two bank vertices carrying (deck_end, bridge, 0|1) under a fresh Bridge, the way stretch between them one straight edge (the deck span); (ii) on each wall run re-traced across the new water (S1 water operator §7.3 (b) 3; a carve crossing a wall §4.11; J-I13), its water gate two bank vertices carrying (gate_end, gate, 0|1) under a fresh Gate, which the Gate record built afterwards names (§2.7); (iii) on the map border line (§3.2 (9)), which must stay closed, its two bank points as anchor contact names, the border stretch between them (one straight edge, or several where the water takes a frame corner or an earlier edit vertex) left across the water unchanged, as a deck span is (the arena outer ring is L0, so new water meets it at its own level); (iv) on every other finer non-way edge the water crosses (settlement-perimeter or other district-boundary stretch, a wall strip setback or glacis line) its two bank points as anchor contact names, the stretch between them removed.

Contact names: a contact name is placed by splitThrough with its row given without an ordinal; the operator names the entity by §2.2 rule 7 and the kernel allocates that entity smallest free anchor ordinal - from 2 on an enceinte, whose 0 and 1 name an open trace ends - as the op applies, in the batch canonical op order, so no two vertices carry one anchor key (§3.10 one-vertex-per-ordinal check); the name lives until the coarse batch strips it (rule 3).

Preparation cut-backs: a coarse chain never shares a finer edge, so a finer edge the new water would run along is cut back by the preparation like any lesser way; a way cut back beyond its bank setback - every lesser way, and a quay or landing, which the operator extends to the new bank only once the water exists, its end an ordinary Steiner vertex on the L0 bank (§4.11 batch (3)) - leaves no contact and needs no prepared vertex. Every stretch the preparation removes (cut stretch, pruned remainder, kept way replaced stretch, stretch between two contact names) is removed through a StretchRef (§3.4); a way left in two parts is first split by retypeEdges rekey on its far part, so role consistency (§3.10) holds after the batch.

Clear region rule 3 Contact: the coarse batch splits the finer faces that meet the region (records re-walked, keeping owners until a later batch of the operator re-owns them), lists the prepared vertices in KernelTx.prepared and may meet finer edges and vertices only there: §3.6 candidate (c) attracts onto each prepared vertex and promotes it. The finer edges at a prepared vertex stay (kept outside the region, the preparation own inside it), so each kept way straight L1 edge between its two promoted bank vertices lies across the new water as the Bridge deck span carrying deck beside way (§2.2 rule 7); each re-traced run edge between its two gate_end vertices is its water gate; the border stretch between its two contact points is the closed frame: no L0 edge crosses the water, no deck splits the water body L0 faces, the way stays one chain through every batch (the structure S1, S3 and S4 build at generation, J-I12). Any other contact with finer geometry is E_LEVEL inside the region and E_KEPT outside it and returns to the dry run (in generation, to the stage property tests). A carve costs its footprint, not the town (re-derivation: §4.11 step 4, §7.3 (b) 8).
The carve fixtures of §13.1-§13.2 confirm the clear-region rules (milestone M3a).

Pre-decided fallback if a carve fixture cannot be met: the batch clears the finer content of its whole L0 land face and re-derives it (the plain rule - correct, slower); moat: all is then carved only before S5c of the outer stage (where L1 holds only arterials), and an edit carve becomes a declared town-wide re-derivation with the fate report (§7.3).

Two op forms (GEO-11; J-K15): a transaction takes exactly one of two forms, fixed by its stage registration (§4.1, §14); a transaction supplying both ops and a callback is a programming error caught by an assertion.

Declared form: KernelTx.ops lists independent ops, none reading another result (S3 carvings, S4 routed arterials, S7 strip lines and furniture, S9 corridorUnion, S11 per-plot footprints, an edit inserted feature). Before applying, the kernel sorts them by a stable key - op kind rank, then the owning entity lineage key (§6.3), then the op index within that entity stream path - so the committed arena is a function of the prior arena and the op SET, not of issue order. Hot-pixel snap rounding is order-independent; attraction, the one order-sensitive rule, is deterministic under the canonical order (op-permutation test §13.1).

Callback form: tx(tx, fn) (§14) hands fn the open overlay; each op fn issues applies at once, in issue order, and later ops read its result (S5c growth queue, S8 bent-cut recursion, S10 plot subdivision are callback-form stages). Issue order is deterministic: a function of the stage inputs, its streams (§6.1) and canonically sorted query results - never slot numbers, worker scheduling or arrival order - and attraction within the sequence follows it (issue-order test §13.2).

No output depends on slot numbers: every kernel tie-break uses lattice positions (y, then x), canonical item keys or entity ids, never a VertexId, HalfEdgeId or FaceId, so an arena compacted on save, one grown through a long session and one merged from pool overlays give identical results for the same next edit (slot-renumbering test §13.1).

Work limits instead of clocks (GEO-2): every op charges operation counts to its transaction (points snapped, attraction queries, placement candidates tried, crossings resolved, faces walked, skeleton events); a transaction exceeding its declared workLimit returns E_WORK_LIMIT. Counts are identical on slow and fast machines, so a budget can select a ladder rung without changing what the seed produces.

The commit record lists what the batch created, changed, moved, promoted, demoted and removed per level; it is the input of the batch-local invariants (§3.10), index maintenance, the display list dirty set (§8) and the digest update - at commit the kernel re-hashes the leaves the batch touched (per-level plat digests and entity leaves) and the nodes on their paths to the root (§6.2, whose budget this keeps). Never persisted (holds arena slots). Commit granularity is part of every stage declaration (§4.1), so the about 48 s hazard of per-insertion commits (engineering judge) and its per-batch twin cannot arise.

The derivation pool overlays (J-K16): the per-district stages that run in the pool (S10, S10b, S11, S12b; §4.1) use these same transactions on DISTRICT OVERLAYS in five steps (frozen base, one overlay per district, scope check, merge, pool size 0).

Pool step 1 The frozen base (J-K25): when the eager S10a and S10 shared-edge step (0) have committed (step (0) runs on the generation worker and builds on both sides at once the bands around every L1 edge two overlays face sets share without corridors, step 3, §4.7), step (0) ends as an eager stage does, by rebuilding the static L3 partitions its batches touched (a finer batch writes no coarser index, so L3 is the only level it touches).

Pool step 1 freeze: at the freeze the generation worker first rebuilds every static partition whose dynamic grid or tombstone set is not empty (none on the one-click path; after edits - an epoch per-district stages, a Re-derive from a stage at or before S10, a verification replay folding either - the partitions the edits left dirty, each holding at most max(256, 1/4 of its static size) grid items) and then asserts every level dynamic grid and every partition tombstone set empty (§3.10). The rebuild is the stage-end rebuild code on live items, changes no output, runs at every pool size, 0 included.

Freeze rebuild costs measured (docs/validation/bench/fixall_kernel_r4_bench.out B): about 2 ms for one district L3 and L4 partitions, about 10 ms for five districts, about 6 ms for the arena-wide L1 partition with one L2 partition, about 59 ms for every partition of a finished CITY. Step (0) own rebuild covers every L3 item it made - at CITY about 9 000 vertices, edges and faces (both sides of about 6 km of perimeter margin band and of the wall band, setback, glacis and tower parts; our count) in about 26 partitions - costing about 2.3 ms at CITY and about 5.8 ms at METROPOLIS (fixall_kernel_r3_bench.out A), carried in §12.4 S10 (0) row.

Pool step 1 copy: the generation worker freezes the arena at that version and sends each pool worker one read-only copy as transferred ArrayBuffers - vertex, half-edge, role and face arrays, the role-head and owner-head tables (typed arrays, §2.2), the index home column and every non-empty level static index partitions (L0-L3 at the one-click freeze, L4 still empty; L0-L4 after edits) - so pooled plot lines ending on a wall band inner edge, setback part or margin band, S12b greenery in setback and glacis residue, and a pooled re-derivation kept locked or pinned content are found by the same indexed queries. No SharedArrayBuffer is used (§11.2).

Frozen copy size: the arena and its tables at most about 12 MB at CITY (§2.2 Size) plus partitions at 38.4 B per item and the home column at 2 B per slot: at the one-click freeze about 60 000-90 000 items (L0-L2 view and step (0) parts; our count, PLAUSIBLE until M1), about 2.2-3.3 MB plus about 0.2 MB home column, so <= about 15 MB per copy and one memory copy of about 1.5 ms per worker (about 4.6 ms for three, measured fixall_kernel_r4_bench.out A); after edits about 20 MB (about 0.5 MB home column; about 2 ms each). §12.4 carries the copies on CITY critical path; §12.8 counts one copy per pool worker.

Pre-decided fallback if M1 memory measurement (or M4 on the epoch path) exceeds the rung line with these copies: a copy made after edits carries only what a pooled stage may read under the laziness contract (§4.1) - the L0-L2 partitions, every L3 partition (step (0) parts are eager) and the L4 partitions of the districts the pool derives (their kept content); another district footprints are lazy output no pooled stage reads - and then §12.8 pool-shrinking step applies.

Pool step 2 One overlay per district: a worker derives each district on a fresh overlay over the frozen base; new vertices, half-edge pairs, face records, role rows and the interned handles of entities the district creates go to the overlay own growable arrays in overlay-local slots numbered above the base high-water mark and are remapped at the merge; a change to a base record (a kerb edge split by a plot line, a face ring re-walked) is a copy-on-write record in the overlay; a frozen-partition item the overlay deletes, re-levels or changes is tombstoned in a set the overlay keeps for that partition (the copy own sets are empty, §3.10), consumed by step 4 district-end rebuild; a pooled stage changes only its district L3 and L4 items. Every district starts from the frozen base alone, never another district overlay, so its result is a pure function of the base, its allocation and its own sub-stream, whichever worker runs it.

Pool step 3 The scope check: a district face set is its L1 faces and every face nested in them; its SCOPE is every face of the set, every edge with a face of the set on both sides, every vertex whose incident faces all lie in the set, and - for a split only (a vertex placed on the edge) - every edge on the set boundary whose other side no overlay writes (a water face, the arena outer ring), so waterfront plot lines may end on their own bank. A write of any kind (split, retype, role row, move, owner change) outside the scope returns E_SCOPE.

Pool step 3 shared edges: the L1 edges two overlays face sets share are never written in the pool: a shared spine is flanked by corridors whose kerbs each side lines end on (avenue and street-tree rows are Greenery.along records in the planting district own half-corridor strips, not roles on the way, §2.7, §4.9); a shared wall trace gets its band, setback, glacis, tower and gatehouse parts from step (0) before the freeze; every other shared L1 edge without corridors (the settlement perimeter between the districts and the hinterland, any reservation boundary two districts share) gets from the same step a margin band (§4.5), so pooled plot and furlong lines end on the band inner edge inside their own set (J-I9).

Pool step 3: the hinterland unit, which the generation worker runs while the pool works, is one more overlay of this kind (§4.1, §4.9). Each overlay also lists the base records it copied; at the merge, two overlays that copied the same base record, or a copied base record the live arena changed after the freeze, fail the pool with E_SCOPE - defence in depth that a test asserts never fires.

Pool step 4 The merge: the generation worker applies overlays in district lineage order (§6.3): new records appended with a slot remap table (overlay-local slot -> next free arena slot), copy-on-write base records replace originals, references rewritten through the remap, only that district faces re-walked to validate rings and parents. The district L3 and L4 static partitions (built by the worker at district end from the base partition live items, step (0) parts included, and the overlay new ones) travel with the overlay, have item tables rewritten through the remap and replace the base partitions with empty tombstone sets, the home column taking their partition numbers, so the merged arena needs no index rebuild. The overlay added and changed role-head and owner-head keys (kept in its own small tables, consulted before the base) are inserted into the live tables through the remap; the district digest leaves (§6.2) travel with it and the root is finalised once after the last overlay.
Merge cost is O(overlay size): the about 200 000 records S10-S12b create at CITY merge within the §12.4 8 ms merge row.

Pool step 5 Pool size 0: the single-worker configuration runs the same overlay-and-merge path inside the generation worker, district by district in lineage order, so pool sizes 0-3 execute the same code on the same inputs and give identical digests by construction; the golden suite pool-size test (§6.5, §13.2) confirms it on every run.

Spatial indexes (SCL-2; J-K6): each level has (a) static packed indexes (flatbush), partitioned - one partition per arena at L0-L1; at L2-L4 one per district plus one for everything outside districts (hinterland, margin) - each with a tombstone set; and (b) one dynamic uniform grid with O(1) insert and delete.
Dynamic grid cell size: 25 m at L0-L1, 10 m at L2, 5 m at L3-L4 (table values).

What each level index holds: the items of that level (current birth level): its vertices; its ROUTE EDGES - each maximal run of that level sub-edges between two vertices of that level or coarser is one item whatever finer vertices later split it, its box the bounding box of the vertices standing on the run when its level batch writes the item, padded by the 0.71 cm hot pixel, and its handle the half-edge leaving its lower (y, x) endpoint (a split keeps that pair on the part at that end, so the handle never changes); and its face records.

Route-edge box completeness: the run box holds every finer vertex on it by construction - one placed afterwards lies within the hot pixel of the route edge (§3.6 placement rule (i)), one placed before stands in the box however the route changed since (§3.6 placement bound; J-K32); the endpoints box, padded alike, missed 38 of 400 753 finer vertices under the placement rule non-nearest choices and the run box none (docs/validation/bench/fixall_kernel_r4_checks.out A).

Index writes by level: a finer batch that splits a coarser edge with a Steiner vertex writes only its own level index (S10 step (0) and every pooled stage touch only L3 and L4 indexes); a promotion or demotion (the coarser batch own change of a route) moves the vertex or edge to its new level index and rewrites the route-edge items of the levels whose routes it changes: a promoted vertex makes the route edge it now splits two items, a demoted vertex joins its two items into one, a demoted edge leaves its old level item for its new level (§2.2 rule 3).

No item changes in place (J-K34): every item a batch deletes, re-levels, changes or moves to another partition - deleted vertex, edge or face; promoted or demoted vertex or edge; a route edge whose run a vertex of its level joins or leaves (same-level split, promotion, dissolution, demotion) or a move reshapes; a vertex a move displaces; a face whose own-level ring a re-walk or move changes; an item whose partition changes (every L2-L4 vertex, route edge and face under an L1 face a batch re-owns to another district or to/from the hinterland - S6 regroup, §7.3 - and a vertex on an L1 edge two partitions share when that edge partitions change) - is TOMBSTONED in the static partition its home entry names (Plat.indexHome, §2.2), if it has one (the entry then reads -1), and its successor, if any, is inserted in the grid of its current level; an item already in a grid is deleted or replaced there.

Consequence of J-K34: a static item is either exact or filtered, and no query sees an item at its old level, place, extent or partition: a promoted-then-demoted plot-line end answers an L2 query not at all and an L3 query once; a regrouped block plots answer once whichever partitions were rebuilt in between; a regroup leaves both partitions dirty, so the next freeze rebuilds both (pool step 1).

Queries: inside a stage every insertion and deletion goes to the grid. A level-n query reads the static partitions of levels <= n its box intersects and their grids, drops each static hit whose item key its partition has tombstoned, expands each route-edge hit into the pieces of its level-n route meeting the box, and returns the vertices of level <= n, each level-n route edge once (as its sub-edge leaving its lower endpoint) and the level-n faces.

Query result order: sorted by the canonical key of each item kind, read on the query level-n route: a vertex by lattice position (y, then x); an edge by the positions of the two endpoints of its level-n route edge, the lower (y, x) first, never a sub-edge endpoints; a face by the positions of the first two vertices of level <= n on its outer ring - the lowest-leftmost vertex of level <= n and the next vertex of level <= n counter-clockwise, finer vertices skipped, and where the ring visits that vertex twice the smaller of its two successors; in a mixed result vertices before edges before faces. The key is total (no two vertices share a lattice point, no two level-n route edges share both endpoints, a face key is one directed level-n route edge bounding exactly one level-n face), so neither which structure holds an item nor whether a finer level was derived changes any answer (a key read on the full ring reverses two L3 plots once S11 derives L4, fixall_kernel_r3_checks.out C); no implementation needs a slot to break a tie.

Defined term TOMBSTONE: an item key - kind * 2^32 + slot, the kind a vertex, a route edge or a face - held in one set per static partition: the items deleted, moved to another level or partition, or changed since that partition build. Tombstones filter that partition hits only; a new item (the next occupant of a slot freed and reused inside the stage, or an item successor) lives in the dynamic grid, which tombstones never filter, so neither slot reuse nor a level change can hide it and the stale static copy never answers (J-K34).

Partition rebuild: indexes the live items belonging to the partition - every item of its level in its arena at L0-L1; at L2-L4 the items of its district, a vertex on an L1 edge two partitions share going to the partition with the smaller key (as §3.9 chunks do) - sets their home entries, removes them from the grid and empties its tombstone set.
Home column: 2 B per vertex, edge-pair and face slot (about 0.5 MB at a finished CITY); lets a batch tombstone an item without searching the partitions.

Static partitions are rebuilt at three moments, never per batch: (1) when a stage ends - an eager stage once after its last batch; S10 eager step (0) once before the pool freeze; a lazy or pooled per-district stage, the district own partitions after that district run; (2) during an editing session, when a partition grid overflow exceeds max(256, 1/4 of its static size) - a count, never an idle timer; (3) at every pool freeze, for the partitions edits left dirty (pool step 1).

Measured flatbush construction (docs/validation/bench/bench_index.out): 0.24 ms at 1 000 items, 2.3 ms at 8 000, 4.9 ms at 17 000; at CITY about one L3 and one L4 rebuild per stage (about 7 ms together) or about 0.2-0.3 ms per district partition, where a rebuild per block or per plot commit would cost 1.9 s (S10) and 13.4 s (S11). A single plot edit rebuilds at most its district L3 and L4 partitions (<= 1 000 items each, about 0.5 ms), inside §12.6 plot-edit budget.
§13.2 cost-model test fails if rebuild work grows with the number of commits.
@plat/kernel ops are the only writers of any arena; tx is the open KernelTx (declared or callback form); write ops charge its work count; writers act at level = tx.level with semantics of §3.6.

insertChain(tx, points: Point[], roles: RoleRow[], cls: mandatory | optional, opts?: { closed?: boolean; pinned?: number[] (chain indices exempt from decimation, §3.6 step 1; does NOT set the kernel pinned flag, which only pinVertices sets); knots?: { index; role: RoleName; ordinal; entity?: Id (default the chain own entity; another entity for a vertex role such as a bridge deck_end or a gate gate_end) }[] (every vertex role row the chain own vertices take) }): KernelResult<ChainInsert>.

interface ChainInsert { placed: VertexId[] } - one per input point, in input order: the vertex the point became after snapping, attraction and sharing (§3.6); valid until the next commit; S11 first wing carry reads it (§2.6).

splitThrough(tx, at: HalfEdgeId, p: Point, row?: RoleRow): KernelResult<VertexId> - a vertex on an existing edge, placed by §3.6 placement rule; a Steiner vertex when the edge is coarser (§2.2 rule 3); row is a vertex role row the placed vertex takes (e.g. a cut end anchor contact name); an anchor row given without an ordinal gets its ordinal from the kernel (§3.3 rule 2); any other indexed row must carry its ordinal, an assertion otherwise.

removeEdges(tx, ref: ChainRef | EdgeSetRef | StretchRef | VertexRef): KernelResult<void> - strips (role, entity) from the ref edges (a StretchRef only after cut knots at its ends) or, for a VertexRef, that vertex role row; deletes edges left with no role; then re-levels and dissolves by §2.2 rule 3, so removing a lane that ended on a spine restores the spine exactly and removing the street a neighbour step served returns the plot-line end it promoted to its level.

clearFiner(tx, faces: FaceRef, level: Level): KernelResult<Conflict[]> - removes content finer than level inside the faces, subject to kept content and, with tx.clearRegion, to clear-region rule 1 (§3.3); kept content stays silently; re-levels and dissolves as removeEdges does; locked or pinned owners are returned, not removed.

retypeEdges(tx, ref: ChainRef | EdgeSetRef | StretchRef, add: RoleRow[], remove: RoleName[], rekey?: { from: Id; to: Id; profiles?: { from?: ChainProfile; to?: ChainProfile }[] (paired by knot role) }): KernelResult<{ profiles: { knotRole; from?: ChainProfile | number | string; to: ChainProfile | number | string }[] }> - the EVO conversion primitive (wall -> way) on role sets; an added row coarser than an edge of the ref is E_LEVEL; remove re-levels as removeEdges does.

retypeEdges rekey: moves the ref (role, from) rows, knot rows and vertex roles to to (for a StretchRef the stretch, its ends being the cut vertices), renumbering each entity knots from 0 in chain order; at every vertex where the moved edges meet edges keeping from it first cuts each profile there (cut knots), and at every vertex where they meet edges already carrying to it joins them (§2.2 rule 5); returns both entities new profiles (a scalar where a part has no knots left), which the caller writes into both records in the same edit.
setOwner(tx, faces: FaceId[], owner: Id): KernelResult<void>.
splitFace(tx, face: FaceId, cut: Point[] (a bent cut is 2-3 vertices)): KernelResult<[FaceId, FaceId]> - children ordered: left of the directed cut first (§3.6).
connectHole(tx, face: FaceId, cut: Point[]): KernelResult<FaceId> - outer ring -> hole slit: same face count, one hole fewer (§3.6).
mergeFaces(tx, a, b): KernelResult<FaceId> - deletes shared partition edges only; a structural shared edge -> E_STRUCTURAL.
absorbSliver(tx, face: FaceId, floor: { minWidthCm; minAreaCm2 }): KernelResult<FaceId> - never deletes a structural edge (§3.6).

claimSubFace(tx, claim: { ring: Point[] } | { areaCm2; within: FaceRef | FaceId[] (as corridorUnion takes: S7b passes a district coarse faces less its wall_strip faces, §4.5); score: RasterRef }, owner: Id): KernelResult<FaceRef> - may span several faces (a reservation crossing coarse faces, a precinct, a bailey).
radialSplit(tx, face: FaceId, apex: Point, raysCdeg: number[]): KernelResult<FaceId[]> - a fan from a centroid or a vertex (groves, chapter houses).
ringBand(tx, face: FaceId, widthCm: Cm): KernelResult<{ band: FaceId[]; core: FaceId }> - an inner band around a court (cloister, quadrangle).

corridorUnion(tx, l1Faces: FaceRef | FaceId[]): KernelResult<BandResult> - the corridor use of bandUnion: L2 half-corridor strips, junction wedges and built blocks for those L1 faces only (§3.7); kept faces inside them are holes (§3.3).

bandUnion(tx, chains: { ref: ChainRef; halfWidthCm: Cm | ChainProfile; ends: round | square }[], faces: FaceId[], edgeRole: kerb | band, owner: Id): KernelResult<BandResult> - the axis chain splits the band per side; corners get corridor_split; a profile is sampled per segment end (§3.7).

warp(tx, field: DisplacementField, fromLevel: Level, region: Point[], recordCheck?: (step: MoveReport) => boolean (the edit layer check of records on the moved ground - held point records §7.4 and carried wings §2.6; false fails the step validation)): KernelResult<MoveReport> - the edit layer computes the field from a WarpStroke or a moveVertex (§7.1), the smoother from a smoothing pass; semantics §3.6.

pinVertices(tx, refs: VertexRef[]): KernelResult<void> - sets the kernel pinned flag and is its only writer: smoothing, simplification and cutting keep the vertex, warp does not (§3.6); released only as §2.2 rule 3 (b) states.

resolve(ref: FaceRef | ChainRef | EdgeSetRef | VertexRef, key: ArenaKey): Resolved - current slots stamped with the arena key and version, valid until that arena next commit (debug build asserts both).

resolveVertexAt(key: PlatKey, at: LatticePoint, sig: VertexSig, carry: CarryMap (§6.3 supersedes table: old address -> successor)): { vertex } | { orphaned: true; nearest?: LatticePoint } - a log position to a vertex, never by distance alone (§2.2 rule 5).
signature(key: PlatKey, v: VertexRef | LatticePoint): VertexSig - what an edit stores beside a position.
sampleProfile(p: ChainProfile, owner: Id, key: PlatKey, atCm: Cm | perVertex): number[] | string[] - a knot profile sampled by arc length along the owner own-level route.
kerb(face: FaceId (L1, committed or in the open overlay)): KernelResult<Ring[]> - §3.7 kerb: what corridorUnion commits.
booleans(op: union | intersection | difference | xor, a: Ring[], b: Ring[], fill: nonzero | evenodd): KernelResult<Ring[]>.

tileRings(rings: Ring[] (world lattice rings, counter-clockwise, in the caller clip order §2.6)): KernelResult<Ring[][]> - the seed clip: per input ring its pieces (the faces of one overlay of all the rings that it contains and no ring before it contains, united), counter-clockwise, none where the rings before it cover it.

buffer(chains: Point[][], halfWidthCm: Cm | Cm[] (per input point of these transient chains), joins: round | square | miter, ends: round | square | flat): KernelResult<Ring[]>. Per-point half-widths apply only to transient chains a caller passes in (a previewed stroke, a skeleton arc); a stored chain varying width is always a ChainProfile sampled by kerb and bandUnion (§2.2 rule 5).
offsetFace(face: FaceId, perEdgeCm: Cm[]): KernelResult<Ring[]> = face minus the union of buffer(edge_i, d_i).
insetRing(face: FaceId, dCm: Cm): KernelResult<Ring[]> - uniform; half-plane path only for a face checked convex (§3.7).
skeleton(rings: Ring[], use: roof | spine | regions): KernelResult<Skeleton> - §3.8: validated output (arcs, nodes with offset times, the face of each input edge) or a typed downgrade.

simplify(chain: Point[], minSegmentCm: Cm, minAngleCdeg: number, obstacles: Ring[], pinned: number[]): KernelResult<Point[]> - Visvalingam-Whyatt, topology-preserving: refuses a removal whose new edge would touch or cross another edge of the ring, its face other rings or an obstacle (checked in the index), or that would move a pinned vertex.
hexLattice(region: Ring[], spacingCm: Cm, jitterCm: Cm, rng: Stream): { points: Point[]; adjacency: Int32Array } - S4 routing lattice with adjacency by construction.

Geometry services: obb(ring), hull(points), lir(ring, axes), sideRuns(face, turnTolCdeg): Run[] (maximal boundary runs with chord directions), sampleBoundary(face, stepCm), pointLocate(key: ArenaKey, level, p), faceNeighbours(key: ArenaKey, face, level), area2(ring), area2Big(ring), orient(a, b, c).
regularFit(ring: Ring): KernelResult<RegularFit> - the ring best-fit regular polygon; §4.8 castle repair and §7.1 equalize brush read it (item 45).

interface RegularFit { n (the ring vertex count); centre {x, y} (the ring area centroid, cm); radiusCm; phaseCdeg (polar angle about centre of the fit corner the ring lowest-leftmost vertex goes to); targets {x, y}[] (per input vertex in input order: its place on the fit, cm - values, never arena coordinates; a caller warp field rounds them at its step, §3.6); compactness (4 pi A / P^2 of the ring) }.

The doors: insertChain is the only door for new edges in a plat (a transient arena opening builds its input rings as exact topology); removeEdges and clearFiner the only doors for removing edges; insertChain vertex rows (opts.knots) and splitThrough row the only doors for adding a vertex role row (with retypeEdges rekey, which moves rows between entities); removeEdges on a VertexRef the door for stripping one (an S8 portal whose lane is removed, §4.6; a tower wallToWay removes, §4.11); warp the only door for moving existing vertices (moveVertex edit = a warp whose field displaces one vertex, resolved by resolveVertexAt; smoothing committed geometry = a warp whose field the smoother computes from the chain current vertices). Every other writer is built from these, so planarity, minEdge, clearance and kept content are properties of this list rather than of every stage (§3.10).
Each op has documented preconditions, work local to the touched faces, a typed result, a declared operation count and fuzz tests with constructive degeneracies (§13.1).
sideRuns gives stages a side notion surviving curved, round-joined kerbs (maximal runs within a cumulative turning tolerance, each with its chord direction), which the bent cut needs (§4.6).

setOwner and retypeEdges are the calls §6.3 succession uses: when a re-derivation hands a carried address to a successor, the same batch re-owns the successor faces and roles under that address, so geometry and address always move together.

Profiled chains: a chain carrying a profile is inserted with its knots (opts.knots: chain index of each knot vertex with its knot role and ordinal); a knot that attraction lands on an existing vertex is carried to that vertex, so the profile keeps its knot. A chain cut into parts owned by different entities, a ring opened, or two chains joined go through retypeEdges rekey, which inserts and drops cut knots by §2.2 rule 5, renumbers each entity knots in chain order and returns the new profiles.

The regular fit (item 45; J-A45.31): regularFit is the ONE computation of a ring best-fit regular polygon so castle repair (§4.8) and equalize warp brush (§7.1) cannot drift apart. Reads the ring counter-clockwise (clockwise in reverse) from its lowest-leftmost vertex p0 through p(n-1); centre c = ring area centroid summed from area2 shoelace terms on bounding-box-relative coordinates in that order, divided through ratio() (§3.2 (6), (8)); first Fourier component a = (1/n) * sum_k (p_k - c) * e^(-2 pi i k / n), each vertex a complex number, summed in ring order; returns radius |a|, phase arg a, and per vertex target t_k = c + a * e^(2 pi i k / n): the regular n-gon about c whose corners lie nearest the ring own in the least-squares sense, vertex k to the fit k-th corner. Targets do not depend on the start vertex (starting one later turns a by one step of 2 pi/n), so the fixed start fixes only summation order. The area centroid (not the vertex average) keeps a side cut into many short edges from pulling the centre.

regularFit numerics: cosines, sines and phase from dmath (§6.5 (2)), lengths from Math.sqrt (exact by specification), so every host returns the same doubles; compactness = 4 pi A / P^2 with A from area2 and P the summed side lengths. The service is O(n), reads no arena and writes nothing.

regularFit callers move vertices toward targets only through warp (§3.6) - whose rounding, whole-step validation, halving and held vertices apply - or, for a ring not yet committed (a castle claim at S3), by building the moved ring and inserting it as any claim; a vertex the caller pins (§4.8 pinned vertices: an on_enceinte claim weld pair and, once the gate is fixed, the two corners of the claim side holding the town-side gate) gets no displacement, while every target is still computed from the whole ring. Degenerate input refused as the §3.1 row states. Fixture: §13.1.

Stretches (J-K31): every operator edit on part of a chain names the part by a StretchRef (§2.2 rule 5) and hands it to removeEdges or retypeEdges, so it passes through the listed doors and their invariant coverage. The op resolves the ref at the batch current state: each end must be a vertex of the chain (named by a vertex role or its lattice point) and both must lie on one part of it, else E_DEGENERATE detail stretch; an end finer than the chain is first promoted to the chain level (W_PROMOTED, listed in the commit record; its split flag cleared), because it becomes an end of the remaining parts.

Stretch removal on profiled chains: removeEdges gives each remaining part of a profiled chain a cut knot at the stretch end on its side (§2.2 rule 5) before the stretch rows and its interior knot rows leave, so every remaining sample is unchanged; retypeEdges rekey cuts at the two ends as at any cut vertex.

A removal that would leave a linear entity in more parts than it declares fails role consistency at commit (§3.10), so an operator cutting a way in two first hands the far part to a new entity with rekey on that part StretchRef. A cut end not yet a vertex is placed first by splitThrough with the vertex role row the operator wants on it (an anchor contact name, given without an ordinal, §3.3 rule 2). Fixtures: §13.1.

Arenas, keys and services (J-A12.32): every writer acts on the arena its transaction key names; every service reading an arena takes it by key: resolve, pointLocate and faceNeighbours an ArenaKey (a PlatKey or a transient arena TransientKey); resolveVertexAt, signature and sampleProfile (which read a plat role rows) a PlatKey. The arenas share no topology (§2.2 rule 2), so an op handed a slot of another arena is a programming error.

Slot stamping: every slot a caller holds comes from a result stamped with its ArenaKey and arena version (Resolved, a query result, a commit record, ChainInsert.placed), valid until that arena next commit (§2.2 rule 5); a debug build carries each slot as a handle stamped with both and asserts wherever passed that its key is the arena the call acts on (the transaction key for an op and for a service handed a slot alone - kerb, offsetFace, insetRing, sideRuns, sampleBoundary, which read the open transaction arena and are called only inside one - the key argument otherwise) and that its version is current, as resolve already asserts. A cross-arena link is an entity id, never a slot.

Cross-arena reads: a stage on one arena reads another through the services alone and never writes it: the underground stage tests what it lays against the ground by pointLocate and resolve on the ground PlatKey (what it tests and what excludes a sample are II.7.3 surface constraint, item 12); a sky island shadow footprint is the same query the other way.
owner_raw: kernel (constraints owned by II.7.3 / V04 underground, V05 sky)

statement: An arena is one planar subdivision: its faces never overlap and two of its chains that cross share a vertex (§3.6 insertion; §3.10 no two edges cross), so inside an arena every crossing is a junction.

The underground layer several arenas (item 65; J-A65.31): underground systems passing over or under one another without meeting (catacomb gallery beneath a sewer main, undercity chamber below tunnels, quarry workings beneath catacomb galleries) never share an arena: each is its own part of the underground layer keyed { layer: underground, part } (§2.2 PlatKey); the sewer network is part 0 (II.7.2); a further system part number is allocated once, when the system is first created, never renumbered or reused (part of its entities keys and addresses, §2.1, §6.3); which system takes which number is II.7.6; inside one part depth stays per entity (J-A12.45), because what shares a part may meet.
owner_raw: kernel (part allocation owned by II.7.6 / V04 underground)

statement: Underground parts add no kernel operation: J-A12.32 holds across parts as between ground and underground; a transaction writes the one part its key names; a stage deriving one system reads the ground and every other part only through the services by key (a catacomb under a churchyard reads the ground faces; where a link to another system can land is a pointLocate in that system part); a place where two systems meet, or a stair or shaft joining them, is a record naming one vertex in each part by its role (II.7.6 link, as AccessPoint names a ground point and a kerb vertex, II.7.4), never a vertex two arenas share.

Every entity faces, chains and vertices lie in the one part its Identity.key names (§2.8), so a FaceRef, ChainRef or VertexRef resolves in one arena - with one exception: a link between two parts (II.7.6 UndergroundLink, §2.7), whose two link_end vertices lie one in each part it joins, each end naming its part ({ part; at }) so resolve reads it with that part key, each placed or stripped by a transaction on that part alone; a grouping spanning systems (an undercity neighbourhood and its outskirts, the plots along the sewer tunnels leading into it, II.7.5) is a link between records in different parts, never one entity with faces or chains in two arenas.
owner_raw: kernel (record UndergroundLink owned by §2.7 / II.7.6 / V04)

statement: Each underground part has its own index partitions (§3.3), snapshot block (§3.9) and level digests under §6.2 per-arena plats node; a system derivation opens transactions on its own part alone, so re-deriving one system leaves the ground and every other part byte-identical (§3.10 arena-isolation row) except the link_end vertices of the links ending on it: the connection stage (II.7.6) re-derives those links, placing, keeping or stripping each far end by one transaction on each part it touches - a link whose element has no successor is removed, its far link_end row stripped by removeEdges on its VertexRef, which by §2.2 rule 3 dissolves the vertex and restores the edge it split unless other geometry met the vertex since.
