Markets over epochs (item 24): a secondary market the roster's suffix adds is claimed by the epoch's S7b in the new stage or in a due district by §4.5 S7b (3)'s rule; a market whose institution closes (the use step) keeps its square — a plaza or market_green — until a clear or a claim reuses it, so no market moves by wealth change alone

Informal clusters over epochs (item 70 (e); J-A70.48): a cluster grows by accretion — delta households of its band placed on an informal plot add structures by §4.7's packing on the plot's free path sites, each a build Works of days (a shack) or less than a week (a tent, finished in its week); rung 1's densify … infill on an informal plot adds structures that way too; a destructive circumstance event (rung 3's trigger) burns a cluster fast — structures decayed and drawn CHARRED in one week, then cleared; when its district's band rises past the hysteresis a cluster is cleared or formalised by rung 3 in the due epoch (replaceability immediate): households re-homed by item 17's relocation or re-let, plot cleared, re-cut by S10 (7) into row-house plots and built by S11 at the new band; in decline, a vacant, cleared or ruined plot of a district whose value fell past the hysteresis takes tenure informal and may take a cluster; each step an event of this section's kinds; the engine scheduling them is the staged one

Lights, deposits and conditions over epochs (items 68, 88): a light follows its host (§4.7 Light sources); an epoch re-runs the light rows on its new and changed faces only; a DepositSite (§2.7; staged, empty in the base) whose state changes converts the land use it anchors: depleted or removed — its quarry, mine or claypit abandoned and drawn worked out (a deposit depleted at creation drawn so from the start); discovered — a new outside site sited by S12a's rows at that epoch; a ConditionOverlay is read as Works (10) states

Strategy registry (§14): every layout stage runs behind a strategy: TerrainStrategy, CoastStrategy, RiverStrategy, ManifestStrategy, NetworkStrategy (the fused base; american/ringed; a village would add a tracker walk), EnceinteStrategy (the base's S5a pull-and-simplify; a village's palisade), FabricStrategy (BentCutFabric now; NG's templates at stage 2), PlotStrategy, SitePlanStrategy, BuildingGenerator (§2.6), EvolutionStrategy (§4.11)

The pipeline order is the topological order of the registered StageDecls (§4.1), so a product may add a stage by registration alone (PART III); every district's SeamContract is complete from milestone 1 (G-P1): the view over the Seam records it shares with its neighbours plus its own boundary plot lines and alleys and interior field samples (II.1); shared geometry is owned by the base; PART II's district → neighbourhood interface reads the contract; nothing in PART II needs a base change; what the base must already carry is listed in II.5 and is a base requirement here

The one placement solver (PlacementSolver, §4.7 S10b) and the designation mutator (DesignationMutator, §4.7 S11) are registry strategies too (§14 StrategyRegistry): a product may register another implementation by name, and S10b, S11, every assignment path (§7.7) and the use step (§4.11) resolve the registered one

The owner-staged layers register the same way — SkyStrategy after S7b, SewerStrategy after S11, and after the network stage UndergroundSystemStrategy (the void systems), UndergroundStrategy (the sewer-front neighbourhoods), UndercityStrategy and last UndergroundLinkStrategy, each by declared I/O (II.6, II.7.3–II.7.6) — and the base registers none of them

§10 plain words: as in FTG every building has a purpose and people: the town starts from how many people live there and what such a town needs (our own tables), places needs onto plots by rules, derives households and people on demand; what drawing and editing need is in the base; hourly schedules, calendar, factions' meetings and events are an optional module over the same ids, so the one-click map never waits for a simulation

Base must-haves (J-9; J-S adopted): the sequential roster (S2) with its need propagation over the supply edges (§4.2 S2, §10.2), the per-plot context vector, the eager allocation (S7b, S10a), the one placement solver with the relation templates (S10b, §4.7), the designation templates and mutator (S11, §4.7), the Use record with its hand relocation path (§2.7, §4.11), households and people derived lazily from their keys, typed open spaces, rule-placed landmarks and furniture, a gazetteer via query

Base schema from M1, materialised by the module: the relation store (family units, relations, memberships, postings), sub-locations, factions with roles and goals, religions, the government's offices (§2.7), and the economy and personality schema stubs of D-32 (§10.3); the supply edges that place a workshop near its suppliers are base placement data (item 16), while prices, stock and trade volumes remain the module's (D-32)

Optional module @plat/sim (delivered at M4b §16; never gating milestone 1, never in the one-click path): professions ↔ workplace matching, occupancy and schedules as a query, the calendar and clock with external time sync, factions' and religions' meetings, events as templates, relations by the family-unit model; schedules and the calendar are not in the base (J-9); restraint: the map stays a clean plan, content in data, hover, the gazetteer and export; one click never asks a questionnaire

The content locality contract (FTG-9; J-P21): content is global and relational while regeneration is spatial: (1) the allocation is persisted and a scoped regeneration re-places only its own scope's allocation — global rebalancing is a separate, reported action; (2) once the module has materialised the relation store, a scoped regeneration changes no relation outside the scope: relations of people whose households were superseded are carried over by the household's address (§6.3) or dropped and reported; (3) the locality oracle and O2 (c) cover content and relation hashes as well as geometry; the relation store's schema is in the base, its data materialised once by the module and then persisted; the one-click path never pays for it

The sequential roster (FTG-14; J-P20): FTG's documented shape, none of its 209 types, 80 nodes, 299 professions or 323 items; a virtual population advances on a fixed grid of Δ = 10 people up to the rung's maximum; at each grid point every class's target count is a monotone step function of the virtual population — perCapita or perOther ratios converted to per-person ratios, core versus shop pools, lifestyle-banded pools with rare outliers (weights ours), hard min/max, size gates (firstAtPopulation), resource gates from SiteResources (no farmland → no farms, shops instead) — every class below its target receives its next building in class-priority then class-id order; every draw keyed by the building's ordinal (roster/<class>/<ordinal>: shop or core, lifestyle outlier), so the n-th chandler is the same at any population; the run records each building's appearance population; manifest(P) = every (class, ordinal) appearing at or below P

Roster prefix stability: manifest(P₂) ⊇ manifest(P₁) whenever P₂ > P₁ (property test on 1 000 seeds, §13.2); an epoch's delta demand is exactly the suffix; a population fall selects the suffix in reverse order; negative deltas arise only from declared circumstance events; §7.8's population control is monotone by construction

Roster mode (COV-FTG-B06): rosterMode 'minimiseUnemployment' (default: at each grid point, when the unemployed share of the virtual population exceeds a table threshold, the workplace class with the largest weighted job deficit receives one extra building) or 'matchRatios' (configured ratios only, FTG's alternative); both grid-sequential, both prefix-stable

Roster output: demand per class with area/frontage requirement classes, district affinities, cluster tags, live-in flags, outside flags and wealth bands; the town-level character shifts the ratios — read from the economy slice's sector shares (circumstances.economy, §7.7 layer 2) through each class's sectors weights, so one input drives both the roster and the neighbourhoods' economy dial (items 72, 78; an even mix, the neutral default, shifts nothing)

An epoch ages everyone by its years through the key's birth epoch; births and deaths are epoch events of the owner-staged evolution engine; when regeneration supersedes a household, its pinned or edited people are fixed inputs re-homed by rule to the household that inherits its address (§6.3), or reported as orphans (their edit-lifecycle row is §7.4's)

(roster class ids)}; ServiceRow {id, providedBy, basePrice}; Stock {building, item, qty}; PriceTable {multiplier, overrides} (global price edits are editTable events §7.6); PersonTraits {traits, motivation, mannerism, hobbies, education} (derived from the person key); StatBlockPack {id, attributes, base, professionModifiers} (a named game-system pack, off by default, D-3)

The naming engine: an original English-fantasy grammar (D-6) in a Tracery-class engine of our own (rules with modifiers, feature guards, weighted decks, conditional lines, article agreement) plus syllable and Markov generators over corpora of our own authoring; folk-contraction as an EVO event (FTG's erosion idea; "≤ 3 syllables" a parameter); names drawn from the naming concerns only (§6.1) and only in §6.3's cases, a successor keeping its predecessor's name and naming record; names never move geometry; uniqueness follows §9.6

Per-culture generators and user lists (COV-FTG-L06): every AncestryRow and culture row names its own grammar and corpora (personal and place names differ by culture); a user-uploaded list (plain text, one entry per line) becomes a user corpus: a syllable and a Markov model trained at load, stored in the document as pack data with author user, selectable wherever a corpus is; selecting it is an adjust of the recipe's pack list entering it as user:<content hash> with shipped: false (§2.9, §7.6), so a town whose history selects it never emits a link (§6.4); the pack holds the corpus and the keyed row operation setting the chosen corpus field of the chosen culture or ancestry row; selecting it re-draws exactly the unedited names drawn from that field, listed for confirmation (§6.3 case (4)), never the row's other names (each corpus field its own naming slice, §7.6); deselecting is a second adjust; how long its content stays is §2.9's pack-set rule

Setting packs (DEF-10): interface SettingPack {id; version; author; date; licence; provides: {grammars?: GrammarDef[]; corpora?: {id; kind: personal|place|word; entries}[]; ancestries?: AncestryRow[]; religions?: ReligionRow[]; appearance?: TemplateDef[]; rosterPatch?: {table: RosterTableId (classes, districtKinds, resources, institutions, government, religions, households, professions, farm, roomProgram, basementGate, covers, classMix, clusters, tenure, quarterIdentities, powerLinks, sectorLinks, bandRanges, sectors; never portRows, which only the dossier port fills); baseVersion; ops: RowOp[] (§7.1)}[]; tablePatch?: {table: TableId (naming, culture and ancestry tables); baseVersion; ops: RowOp[]}[]; styleHints?: Partial<StyleSheet>}}

A pack is data, never code: schema-validated (zod), every entry carrying author and date (clean-room rule §17), loaded as one layer of the override chain between the shipped defaults and the preset (§7.6), recorded in the recipe or in the adjust that adds it by id, version and content hash; the content of every pack of the document's pack set not shipped with the output version is copied into the document's packs block and retained by §2.9's pack-set rule, so a replay never depends on what is installed; a link emitted only when every pack of the pack set is shipped (§6.4)

A pack's roster patch and table patch are keyed row operations, never positional — the RowOps of §7.1, each set carrying the hash of the base row it was written against (baseRowHash) and the table version it targets (baseVersion), orphaned and reported exactly as a user override is (§7.6; LC-22) — so a newer table version never silently misapplies a pack; a user corpus pack is {corpora: [the uploaded list], tablePatch: [one set on the chosen culture or ancestry row's corpus field]}; the base ships exactly one pack, our original English-fantasy set; further packs are the owner's adopted default "setting packs later" (D-6); adding one is a file, not a code change

Names follow character (item 72 (c)): S13a names a district from its identity (§4.5 (4)): the identity row's naming slice, whose feature guards read the district's dominant components — its trade (Tanners' Row), anchor institution (Temple Hill), power (the Guildquarter), gate or trade bearing (the Northgate — the gate of the largest trade weight among its routes, §4.3) or terrain; a name once given is kept: a district whose identity changes past its hysteresis at an epoch re-draws its name on its naming stream by §6.3's epoch case (J-A72.44), the old name kept in District.nameHistory (the reader shows it as a former name; the change reported); a protected name (setAttr, lock, assignment, claimed name) never re-drawn; a quarter node's name reads its members' dominant identity (§9.1)

Claimed quarter names (item 82): a quarter the dossier names becomes the name of whichever district §7.7's claim rule matches, protected as an assigned name (§2.8's dormant naming record) and re-matched only past §4.5 (9)'s identity hysteresis; an unmatched claim waits, reported, never forced (§7.7)

Stage words (item 67): a building's description reads its Works stage at the drawn week: "being built", "being extended", "being demolished", "under repair", or "ruined since" the calendar year of the ladder event that ruined it (§4.11)
An informal cluster (item 70) takes one place name from our naming pack's cluster slice, drawn once for the cluster plot on its naming stream, and one label (§9.1); its structures unnamed

An undercity neighbourhood (item 65; J-A65.40) is named as the underside of its parent's quarter — our naming pack's undercity slice, whose grammar reads the parent quarter's name (the Under-⟨quarter⟩, ⟨quarter⟩ Below …) — drawn once on its own naming stream, a quarter node under its parent's (§9.1; II.7.5); re-drawn only in §6.3's cases, so a later rename of the parent quarter leaves it standing

PART II plain words: any district can be opened as a detailed neighbourhood (like watabou's Neighbourhood) with blocks, plots, courtyards, hatched roofs, wells, local street names; the base draws every shared street, wall and shore exactly once, so two neighbourhoods never disagree about their common edge; each district has its own random stream, so re-rolling one never touches another; the neighbourhood's look is a closer LOD of the same picture; Neighbourhood's four templates become layout choices per district: area is the base's bent-cut fabric, street, square, ring are template fabrics laid by the same engine (II.2)

interface Seam (one per boundary run, created by S6, read by both districts it separates, from milestone 1, G-P1) {id; sides: [Id, Id|null] (two districts in address order; null a one-sided run — frame, water, cliff, sky); edges: SeamEdge[] (in the first side's ring order; each {chain: ChainRef (shared way, shore, wall, reservation-boundary or perimeter chain), type: way|water|wall|reserve|field|cliff|frame|sky, reservation? (reserve only), wayClass?, widthCm?, frontageSide?, hard: boolean}); portals: Portal[] (every way crossing or meeting the run: {id, wayId, class, widthCm, at: VertexRef ('portal', id), bearing, from: growth|baseLane|closeup, by?: Id} — every one must be connected); amendments: SeamAmendment[] (vertices inserted on a shared spine after S6: S8's lane ends and close-up T-junctions — one record so both sides agree); boundarySamples: {prosperity; density; greenery; terrain: Sample[]} (hard seams jump, soft interpolate)}

interface SeamAmendment {kind: baseLane|tJunction; spine: Id (shared boundary way); vertex: VertexRef (('junction', new junction id): inserted at level 1 by splitThrough or as a lane's end); portal: Id; by: Id (district whose batch inserted it); cause: 'generation' | EditId (S8's run, a regenerate, or the close-up's event)}

interface SeamContract (a district's view assembled on demand from its Seam records; never stored) {district; seams: Id[] (ring order); sharedGeometry: 'ownedByBase' (shared edges generated once by the base; neighbourhoods change them only through a SeamAmendment); plotLinesOnBoundary: EdgeSetRef[]; alleysOnBoundary: Id[] (resolved from the district's own plots and alleys); interiorSamples: {prosperity; density; greenery; terrain: Sample[]} (on an interior lattice)}

interface NeighbourhoodRequest {district; key: PlatKey (ground, the sky island's arena, or an underground part — layer underground: the sewer's part 0 or an undercity neighbourhood's void part); boundary: TypedBoundary; seam: SeamContract; context: DistrictContext (kind, venue mix, character, prosperity band, growth stage, water, walls, slope); laid: {blocks; plots; alleys} (the base's own L2/L3 fabric under this district); layer: ground|sky|underground (sky: no portals, no roads in or out, own terrain optional; underground: the underground close-up); mode: refine|replace (refine presentation detail only, derived; replace a template fabric, a model edit, II.4); strategy: FabricStrategyId ('bent-cut' (refine; NG's area template) | 'ring' | 'square' | 'street' (replace)); params: Record<string, number>; outlineTemplate?: disc|d_shape|lozenge|crescent|spindle (standalone and sky calls only, §4.2 S1 (2)); streams keyed from the district's lineage on demand (§6.1), nothing stored; lod: 'neighbourhood'}
interface NeighbourhoodResult {blocks; ways; plots; buildings; greens: Greenery[]; pins: Pin[]; labels: LabelEntity[] (§9.1); seams: SeamReport; report: StageReport}

interface SeamReport (written by every close-up; its numbers are stage-2 feature S1's acceptance, II.5) {portalsTotal; portalsConnected (must equal portalsTotal); unconnected: Id[]; addedPortals: SeamAmendment[]; sharedEdgeHausdorffCm (must be 0: shared edges read from the base; an amendment only inserts a vertex); fieldJumps: {at: PointCm (a sample position, not a vertex); field: prosperity|density|greenery; delta; hard}[] (a jump on a soft seam outside its band is a soft-invariant failure); superseded: {old; new}[] (§6.3's successions for entities a template replacement re-derived; anchor rule §2.1, §6.3)}

interface NeighbourhoodStrategy {generate(req: NeighbourhoodRequest, ctx: StageContext, k: Kernel): KernelResult<NeighbourhoodResult>}; Pin is defined in §2.7 (complete furniture vocabulary, in the entity registry from M1)

Seam records (J-P33): one Seam record per boundary run, read by both districts it separates, so the two contracts cannot disagree and a district's re-derivation changes only the seams it is party to (§4.6, II.4)

Seam edge types (J-P37): an edge's type is the first its role rows give: way → way; wall → wall; shore or bank → water, or cliff where the bank kind is cliff; reserved → reserve; district_bound alone (the settlement perimeter) → field; border or margin → frame; a sky arena's outline → sky

A reserve run is a reservation boundary two districts share with no way on it (a plaza's, precinct's or market's edge where the grower's edge test stopped, §4.5): its shared geometry is the reserved chain and the two parts of §4.5's margin band along it; no portals; a close-up ends its plot lines on its own part's inner edge and writes neither part (a replace close-up's scoped regeneration re-lays its own side's part, §7.3 item 2)

hard comes from the seam-type row of the editable tables (§7.6): wall, water, cliff, frame and sky hard; way and field soft; reserve by the reservation's kind — castle and precinct hard; plaza, market, park and institution soft

II.1 rules (1) the base generates every shared edge once and both districts read it; (2) a close-up either refines — adds neighbourhood-LOD presentation detail (roof construction and hatching, surfaces, pins, trees, local street names) as a pure function of the district's committed base state, sub-seed, strategy and params, never changing L1–L4 geometry — or replaces the base's plots with a template layout inside its boundary with ring/square/street; templates are FabricStrategy registrations selected per district (G-P2), so a template district is laid by the base's own engine with seams by construction

II.1 (3) seam amendment (GEO-30): a close-up may end a street on a shared boundary spine (NG's cuts end on existing roads, 361/361; the ring template's radials run to the edge); each such end a T-junction inserted with splitThrough at level 1, so the shared spine stays one chain, recorded as a SeamAmendment (kind tJunction) and a new portal in the shared Seam record

The neighbour step (J-P38), the only write on the other side, the same for a close-up's T-junction and a lane a district's reroll adds or removes on a shared spine (§4.6 step 7): one L2 batch whose only face is the neighbour's half-corridor strip along the split spine edge inserts one corridor_split edge from the junction vertex to the foot of its perpendicular on the neighbour's kerb (the edge corridorUnion builds on a side the spine passes straight through, §3.7), so each spine sub-edge keeps its own strip (§2.2 rule 1) and that side gets no wedge; a half-corridor strip holds no L3 content (avenue and street-tree rows are Greenery.along records), so the batch clears and re-derives nothing

Neighbour step kerb landing: the edge's kerb end lands by §3.6's attraction on a vertex of the kerb's route within attractCm — a plot-line end or footprint corner there promoted to L2 (§2.2 rule 3): every ring of the vertex's own level and finer stays, each coarser ring along the kerb gains it (the neighbour's block at L2, its plot at L3 when the promoted vertex is an L4 footprint corner) — or otherwise splits the kerb at L2 by the placement rule, adding that one vertex to the rings through it and, by §2.6's wing-carrying rule, to the wing ring of a building whose footprint fronts that stretch; each changed ring equals its prior ring with the vertex removed (II.4's seam exception)

Neighbour step reversal: removing the street reverses the step (undo, the district's reroll or any later edit): removeEdges takes the corridor_split out, the strip is one face again, a kerb vertex the step created dissolves (split flag, no role) and leaves the wing ring it joined, a plot-line end or footprint corner the step promoted returns to its level by demotion — it kept its split flag, which only a warp that has since moved it or the kerb vertices beside it clears (the bend becoming part of the kerb's true shape, §3.6) — so the kerb's L2 route, index and digest and every ring the step touched are those before the step, with any later change to the kerb kept (§2.2 rule 3; test §13.1); every portal stays connected (stage-2 feature S1's acceptance: portal connection 100 %, shared-edge Hausdorff 0; II.5)

II.1 (4): footprint hashes at city LOD and neighbourhood LOD identical for every entity a refine close-up covers (refinement never changes geometry); close-up persistence is II.4's; a replace close-up re-derives its entities under the anchor rule and records §6.3's successions in SeamReport.superseded

II.1 (5): the standalone no-portal mode is the same call with a synthetic boundary from an outline template (§4.2 S1 (2); NG's template outlines, our own shapes; COV-NG-N06) through §4.2's closed-outline routine; the sky-island call is the same request with layer 'sky', an outline from that routine, optional own terrain echoing the ground, no roads in or out, and a reason (II.6), its shadow projected onto the ground by §8.4

II.1 (6) Base lanes on shared spines: the lanes the base's own S8 ends on a district-boundary spine are the same kind of vertex, recorded in the same Seam record with kind baseLane and kept at least a portal gap from every other portal on the spine (§4.6 step 7), so a close-up reads them like any portal and a reroll of either district changes only the seam records it is party to, the vertices it inserts or removes and their neighbour steps (3) (II.4)

Close-ups and the geometry floor (item 31): a refine close-up reads the committed plots and changes no plot record (builtBand included); a replace close-up is a model edit of the redevelopment class (II.4): the plots its template lays take builtBand and builtProsperity from the band and value the template read, as a rung-3 event of §4.11 does

The underground close-up (II.7.3): with layer 'underground' the underground pseudo-district opens as a refine close-up — key the sewer's part (part 0 of the underground layer), no portals, no roads in or out, its tunnels the ways its plots front, no replace fabric; an undercity neighbourhood (II.7.5) opens the same way — a refine close-up with key its void's part, walkways the ways its plots front, no portals, no replace fabric

RingFabric (COV-NG-N12): concentric secondary ring roads inside the boundary at a radius law (a table) are the template's only seed geometry, no template radials; ring courses (default; item 58 (a); provenance ref:NG 1.2.2 ring courses (code), P19): the radius law's default row lays rings from the district's ring centre (area centroid) outward: first spacing = the district's lower block extent e_lo (§4.6 step 1) plus a uniform share of the radius remaining to the boundary's inset; each further spacing = previous × (1 + f), f the folded four-uniform bell of §4.6 step 1 (a per-ring factor in [1, 2)), rings widening outward; a ring whose course would leave the boundary's inset is not laid; outermost band runs to the boundary; each ring a hexagon at its radius — every ring sharing one phase drawn once per district, each vertex's radius moved by a centred bell of ringJitter × the ring's spacing — smoothed by ringPasses corner-cutting passes (each corner replaced by the points at ¼ and ¾ of its two edges; three passes take the hexagon to 48 vertices); draws on cut.arc keyed by district and ring ordinal (§6.1; no new concern)

Ring template uncut centre: the face inside the innermost ring is laid out at equal odds as a square, a green block or a manor block; where the district's greenery rows allow no greens and no trees the ring nearest the centre is closed instead as a loop around a plaza; ringJitter (0.15, own) and ringPasses (3, P19) are the ring template row's values, settable per district through fabricParams by setAttr (II.4); jitter share recalibrated on M5's NG ring pairs (J-S34); for scale only: NG's medium area template spans ≈ 525 m (export scale 0.35 m per unit) — descriptive, an inference Fable's evidence gate released as such (item 58 (f)); no default derived from it

Ring bands processed outside-in, one hole-aware bent-cut recursion per annulus (§4.6's slit and holed position law): the band's first cut is a slit opening the annulus without splitting it; its later cuts are its radial streets arriving at the ring roads at right angles; each band draws its cuts from its own sub-stream, so radials are staggered band to band, never one straight line through all rings (NG RA-2, RA-4, PF-1); radials of the outermost band reaching the boundary use II.1 rule (3)'s seam amendment

SquareFabric: mode 'carved' places a rectangular or round plaza face at the district's centroid or at a portal, sized from population, frontages typed square, then the bent cut on the remainder; mode 'void' (COV-VG-VN-179) carves nothing — plots whose frontages face a chosen open area are left unbuilt, the square the irregular void their omission forms; in both modes a centrepiece pin (monument, statue or fountain; COV-NG-XB23) at the square's nexus; the square template row's default is mode 'void' (J-S42) — a district opened with square and no mode, and every square pair of the D-5 panel against NG (§13.6 (2)), gets the void; carved recorded as fabricParams.squareMode = 1 (0 or absent is void, since fabricParams holds numbers, §2.5), set by setAttr (II.4)

StreetFabric: a main street between two portals with plots directly on it, bent cuts on the deeper faces; template road widths (COV-NG-N20): ring roads and template streets take fixed per-district widths drawn once from the district's stream (NG draws them as its per-map maximum), cut streets follow §4.6's width law; a template is its seed geometry plus the number of sub-areas it hands to the bisector (CA-2) — a data row plus a strategy class

The area template is the base's own bent-cut fabric (FabricStrategyId bent-cut, §4.6), the default, opened as a refine close-up; templates chosen by context (stage-2 feature S4) read the district context (a quay district a quay-parallel street; an intramural district a ring near the wall; a stepped street on a slope)

II.3 block content dispatch (stage-2 feature S2): a stage-2 table maps (block area, spacing to the nearest green, spacing to the nearest landmark or manor block, district kind, prosperity band) → the weighted choice among ordinary, manor, empty and green blocks that NG also makes (B6); NG greens a court whenever its frontage ring is complete (green share follows block and lot sizes, 23–58 % of ordinary blocks) — ours has a target per band from §4.9's rules (item 58 (b)); a minimum landmark spacing row keeps landmark and manor blocks apart (COV-NG-XA07)

Neighbourhood-tier pins (wells, fountains, large trees, statues, monuments, bandstands) placed in yards and squares by a probability gate per kind and band, the chosen kind's weight divided by 10 for the rest of the block's picks so one block rarely repeats a kind (item 58 (c); provenance ref:NG 1.2.2 pin decay (code), P20; drawn on pin.decor keyed by the block and pick ordinal), as refine-mode presentation detail; the base's own pins (§4.7 S11) are model entities at every LOD

Local street identities (names, surfaces, widths) from the way records and naming grammar; context features (stage-2 feature S2: quays, intervallum along the wall, stepped streets, bridge approaches) are constraints inside the boundary; a manor compound's enclosure wall and gate are the base's PlotBound treatments (§2.5, §4.7 S11), so the close-up draws a compound's enclosure from model data (ours, extension; NG's manors stand unenclosed; COV-NG-N27, item 44)

The prosperity band the dispatch reads is the block's manifested band — §4.11's block-level reading of its plots' geometry floor (item 31; J-A31.43) — while a pin's probability gate reads the field band

Render tier (stage-2 feature S5): the hatched preset at neighbourhood LOD is §8.2's and §8.6's (hatching from the ridge, two-tone roofs over stored wings, prism shadows from stored heights, chimneys, wells, lobed trees ordered as NG orders them — large-tree pins under buildings, block trees above (item 58 (d); §8.2 layer note)); at this tier it adds cobbles/tiles/outlined/dashed road programs and the hood title in the emptiest corner (§9.5), with instanced hatching and a ceiling of ≈25 canvas ops per wing

Persistence status (LC-18; J-P23): a refine close-up is derived data — pure function of the district's committed base state, sub-seed, strategy and params, identical eager or lazy, held outside the base hash, never stored; the first edit inside a close-up is preceded by a logged closeup event (strategy and params, §7.1), from which point the close-up enters the digest under closeups (§2.9) and replays exactly; editing a close-up element (moving a well, removing a tree, restyling a pin) records an instance-override event on the element's host entity and ordinal (§7.1), which persists, undoes and replays after regeneration, re-matched by position; when the base re-derives the district the close-up re-derives with those overrides carried and orphans reported; close-up lanes, plots and houses are base entities (renaming a lane or locking a house an ordinary base edit)

A replace close-up (template fabric) is a model edit: setAttr(district.fabric, template) plus a scoped regeneration of the district — logged, hashed, the same for every viewer, visible at city LOD because city-LOD footprints read the same model

Workflow (stage-2 feature S6): open any district at neighbourhood LOD from the city view; "Same kind, new seed" per district with locks — New random on the district (§7.1 named action scoped to it); per-district reroll isolation (R8): rerolling D leaves every other district byte-identical except the seam exception — D's bounding ways' chains and Corridor records, the strips, wedges and neighbour steps at vertices D's batches insert or remove on those spines, the neighbouring rings through those vertices (each the same polygon point for point with them removed) and the Seam records D is party to — stated in full in §7.3 item 1; the locality oracle computes this set from the batches' commit records and checks everything else byte for byte; II.5's reroll-isolation tests check it; export of one district as its own SVG/PNG/VTT scene

Elaboration by click at stage 2 (item 28): opening a district follows §4.1's trigger policy: in click mode the click derives the close-up and raises the wings rung of its buildings to current (§2.8); in view mode visible tiles derive within §12's budgets; model the same either way, persistence status unchanged (a refine close-up stays derived data); staleness, the change marker and the click's re-derivation are §4.1's policy over §2.6's rule (§7.3): a stale close-up re-derives as a pure function of its district's committed state (§6.2), a stale rung from its canonical prior, never from the cache, never a re-roll

II.5 What the base already carries for stage 2: typed boundary edges with hard flags and portals in the shared Seam records of every district (§2.5, II.1), the lane ends S8 puts on boundary spines included (§4.6); shared geometry owned by the base (§2.2) with the seam-amendment protocol and splitThrough (§3.4, II.1); plot lines and alleys on the boundary (§4.7); seam-continuous prosperity, density and greenery fields with hard/soft seams (§4.5); per-district streams keyed from each district's lineage (§6.1); the hole-aware bent cut with its restated recipe (§4.6); the FabricStrategy slot (§14, G-P2) with BentCutFabric registered from M1 and the three template fabrics at M5; stored wings, boundary treatments and the complete pin vocabulary (§2.5–§2.7); the neighbourhood LOD band declared in the display list and the hatched programs (§8); the world-aligned tile pyramid (§8.8) invalidated by per-district dirty regions; the per-district regeneration budget (§12.6); the close-up persistence rule and instance-override event (II.4, §7.1); the sky context and outline templates (§2.1, §4.2, II.6)

Stage-2 readiness of the base itself (M1 exit, before any close-up generator): on every B-CITY city every district's SeamContract view resolves completely — every boundary run belongs to exactly one Seam record, every seam edge carries one of II.1's types (a way-less reservation boundary between two districts as reserve, with its two margin-band parts), every portal's vertex resolves, every baseLane portal matches exactly one S8 lane end and every lane end on a boundary spine one baseLane portal — 100 %; and a New random on each of 20 districts per city changes nothing outside its seam exception (II.4)

Stage 2 itself (M5 exit, §16), read from II.1's SeamReport — stage-2 feature S1's acceptance: portals connected 100 % (added portals included); shared-edge Hausdorff distance 0; field jumps on soft seams within band; footprint hash at neighbourhood LOD identical to the city-LOD hash for every entity a refine close-up covers; opening a district ≤ NG's recorded 10–96 ms at comparable counts, and per-district regeneration ≤ 30 ms (§12.6); rerolling one district leaves every other district byte-identical outside the seam exception (II.4); the model hash unchanged by opening, closing or reopening any number of districts
Per-district regeneration ≤ 30 ms (§12.6); opening a district ≤ NG's recorded 10–96 ms at comparable counts

The elaboration record per rung (§2.8) and the elaboration cache (§2.9), with the elaborate view key (§4.1) and the stale marker (§8.5): the base's carriage of item 28's click policy, which stage 2's close-ups and stage 3's rungs share

II.6 plain words: the owner stages both layers after the city is mastered; whether a layer exists is a model rule (the island rule; II.7.1's tier row), and its layer toggle shows it; nothing here built in the base, but every record and interface exists now, so adding them later is a registration, not a redesign

Floating islands (AM-2; DEF-7): a settlement has 0–3 islands by the island rule — with the model setting on, the rung, count slots and supply decide them; the view toggle only shows them; why an island exists is one of two reasons, by rule or assignment: prosperity — the island carries a very prosperous neighbourhood or set of neighbourhoods: by rule (recipe.layers.islands on, rung admits islands, a count slot opens) S7b (5) allocates the roster's richest demand to that slot's sky pseudo-district under the supply law (5), so the population stays whole; institution — the island carries one unique institution chosen from an IslandInstitution row (a palace overlooking the land, a cathedral, a prison isolating criminals) or named by an assignment

What an island is: a SkyIsland (§2.7) with an organic oval outline from §4.2's routine (an outline template of §4.2 S1 (2)), an altitude from the supply law (5), optionally its own terrain from S1 run on the sky plat with an echo request — relief echo or own, a conjured river taking the ground river's bearing and width law; its districts laid by the ordinary pipeline through a NeighbourhoodRequest with layer 'sky' (no portals, no roads in or out; II.1 (5)); where it floats: a placement rule reads the ground plan — over water, fields or outskirts by default, over the built core only by assignment (SkyIsland.placement, §2.7); occlusion mode (opaque, ghost the covered ground, offset view) a rendering choice (§8.4); no relation to the underground layer; exports as its own layer (§11)

Island light and shadow (item 68): in §8.4's lighting model an island casts shadow from above — an occluder slab with a top and an underside, shadow falling from its underside onto whatever lies below; the ground under it shaded from above yet lit from the side; its magical lights are the sky rows of §4.7's light table (LightRule, arena sky), strength scaled by the island's supply h(S_carried) — a waning island's lights fade with it; hook interfaces IslandRule and SkyStrategy have one declaration each

Sewers (DEF-7): a SewerStrategy registers as a stage after S11 (declared inputs: ways with flowToward, the drainage raster and outfalls of §2.3, plots and buildings with their class table's drain column, the underground plat; output: Tunnel records §2.7); rule families are data: follow-streets (mains under the ways, falling with flowToward to the outfalls), drainage-lines (along natural drainage), mixed; which buildings need drains is the class table's column; two presets — historical (restrained: open gutters, a few culverted mains, cess pits by class) and navigable (the fantasy preset: large vaulted mains with chambers); renders through the ground by §8.4's cut-away or overlay and exports as the underground layer
interface SewerStrategy {derive(doc: Document, rules: {family: follow-streets|drainage-lines|mixed; preset: historical|navigable}, ctx: StageContext, k: Kernel): KernelResult<Tunnel[]>}

The island rule (owner quotes: prosperity, magic a supplied resource, limited to cities and metropolises, not all have them; AM-10, AM-13, AM-15): one rule decides whether a settlement has islands, how many and how large; the toggle only shows them; its rows are band rows of the coverage/granularity/greenery family (§4.7, §4.9), interpolating along the prosperity value and reading the same field (§4.5)

(1) Two settings, not one: recipe.layers.islands ∈ {off, on} is a MODEL setting — off by default, the named fantasy toggle of D-3 (realism base has no island; ground model byte-identical to the realism golden); changing it is an adjust of the recipe that re-derives from S7b (§7.6, §7.7; control row §7.8's); the sky layer's LayerSpec.visible (§8.4) is the VIEW toggle: shows the islands a settlement has and creates none; a hidden island still exists and carries its households; hiding or showing leaves the model digest unchanged (J-A15.41)

(2) The gate — rung: islands possible only where RungProfile.layers.islands (§1.1) allows: none at TOWN and every village rung (PART III), possible at CITY and METROPOLIS; the rung is the one the request's population chooses at generation and, in an epoch, the one the epoch's population target chooses (§4.11), so a settlement leaving the CITY band can no longer sustain islands and one entering may gain them (J-A13.41)

(3) The supply: an island's existence and size are functions of two prosperity values from §4.5's field: S_town = area-weighted mean prosperity over the settlement's built land (one scalar per town, recomputed per epoch); S_carried = mean band value of the households the island carries (S7b (5) fills from the richest band down); supply function h(v) a band row per rung interpolated along the value: 0 up to threshold τ — the lower cut the town's FieldBands record for the thresholdCut band, prosperous by default — rising to 1 at the rich band's top; no island where h(S_town) = 0; none carried where h(S_carried) = 0; an institution island reads the same gate: exists only where h(S_town) > 0, its S_carried its institution's requirement band (J-A10.41)

(4) The count: 0–3 islands drawn once per town on island.place (§6.1) before any allocation, from three ordered slots: slot k opens with probability chance_k · h(S_town) and only if slot k − 1 opened (defaults 0.6, 0.5, 0.35), so a poor city has none, a rich one may have none or several; count depends on seed and prosperity, never on the toggle (J-A15.42); an epoch re-draws the slots with the epoch component, each slot at the per-year rate redrawPerYear (default 0.1, own) converted to the epoch's span as 1 − (1 − redrawPerYear)^years, power by dmath.pow (§6.5 (3); §4.11's per-year rule, item 67; J-A67.40), so a weekly epoch re-decides a slot no more often per year than a decade-long one; a slot that opens raises a new island only where supply admits one (raiseIsland); a slot that closes is read by the decline ladder, never an instant removal

(5) Size and altitude: for an open slot the supported area A = areaHaMax(rung) · h(S_carried) · h(S_town) and altitude elevationCm = E_min + (E_max − E_min) · h(S_town) (area from both prosperities, altitude from the city's alone; J-A10.43); S7b (5) fills the island's allocation from the richest band down until the plot land of A (× dense core's plot share, §4.2 S2) is used or three districts' worth of households are allocated, recomputing S_carried and A as it adds (A falls as poorer households join, so the fill converges); no allocation for a slot whose A is 0; SkyStrategy sizes each outline to its allocation's area and floats it at its altitude

(6) Over epochs (§4.11): supply re-evaluated each epoch; an island whose A shrinks by more than the hysteresis (0.05 of its area) is resized; one whose h(S_town) or h(S_carried) falls to 0 wanes, settles and falls; regrowth re-floats a settled island before raising a new one (J-A10.42); an island's lifecycle state is SkyIsland.state (§2.7)

(7) Editable: the count, each island's area and altitude and its state are attributes under setAttr and lock (§7.1, §7.2); resizeIsland, settleIsland, fallIsland, refloatIsland and raiseIsland are convert events a user may apply by hand; every draw on island.place, so an edited island survives regeneration by §6.3's rules; (8) emulation: no reference has islands; with the model setting off nothing runs

interface IslandRule (one row per rung that admits islands; read by S7b (5) and SkyStrategy; a rule table §7.6) {rung: CITY|METROPOLIS; chance: [n, n, n] (three ordered slots, each × h(S_town)); thresholdCut: prosperous|rich; supply: {band; h}[] (h(v) per band row); areaHaMax; elevationCmBand: [Cm, Cm]; placement: (water|fields|outskirts)[]; terrain: none|echo|own; institutions: IslandInstitution[] ({kind, requirementBand, areaHa}); hysteresis (share of area; default 0.05); dwellYears: [n, n] (waning → settled, settled → fallen); redrawPerYear (item 67; default 0.1)}

interface SkyStrategy {place(doc, rule: IslandRule, allocations: Allocation[] (S7b (5)'s sky allocations: open slots with A > 0, each with supported area and altitude), ctx, k): KernelResult<SkyIsland[]>} — a Stage registered after S7b by declared I/O: inputs the sky allocations and the ground plan; outputs the islands (outline sized to the allocation's area, placement by rule), their arenas and districts, which run the ordinary pipeline through a NeighbourhoodRequest

The underground fades like the walls (owner quote; AM-11): a tunnel's lifecycle is a ladder like a wall's, moved only by §4.11's lottery at the underground's persistence rate — after streets and walls, before terrain and water (J-A11.42) — and by hand: in use → neglected, silted (abandoned) → partly caved in (decayed) → collapsed or decommissioned, sealed (ruined, with Tunnel.closure ∈ {collapsed, sealed}, §2.7); conversions silt, caveIn and seal act on one tunnel record — DeclineOp's element names it (§4.11; an older convert event's tunnel field reads as element, §7.5) — and reopen undoes them

Tunnel stretch conversion (J-A11.43): a conversion given a stretch first widens it at both ends out to the first centreline vertex at or beyond that end whose station no underground plot's frontage straddles on either side (a plot's frontage read as the interval of centreline stations its frontage edges project onto) — a vertex where frontages break on both sides, a junction or the tunnel's end — so no plot fronts two records (U1, II.7.3), the widening shown by the dry run and reported with the event's fates; then splits the tunnel at the stretch's two ends, handing the stretch (and for an interior stretch the part beyond it) to new Tunnel records by rekey on their StretchRefs (§3.4), as a cut way hands its far part (§4.11 carve): each part keyed by §6.3's SPLIT rule, each keeping the record's attributes on its own stretch (invert knots, outfall at its end, plots and buildings whose connections meet it, its chambers Tunnel.chambers, access points whose vertex lies on it AccessPoint.under.element, II.7.4); the Frontage records of the underground blocks along it split wherever one spans a stretch end, in the same step (each part beyond an end a new record, its kerb edges' ('frontage', id) rows moved by rekey, each part's lengthCm its own, keyed by §6.3's split-Frontage rule) and each re-pointed (Frontage.way) to the part it fronts; an undo restores the one tunnel record and each split Frontage's one record (§7.4)

Tunnel condition table (one statement of a tunnel's condition, read by §2.7's Tunnel, §2.8's decline hooks and II.7.3): in use — existence generated, built, altered or converted; closure —; open yes; reached by generation or a drawn tunnel, reopen from any other condition · neglected, silted — abandoned; —; yes; silt on a run in use · partly caved in — decayed; —; no; caveIn on a run in use or neglected · collapsed — ruined; collapsed; no; caveIn on a partly caved-in run · sealed (decommissioned) — ruined; sealed; no; seal on a run in any other condition · flooded (galleries and chambers of II.7.5 and II.7.6 only, item 65) — ruined; flooded; no; flood on an element whose floor lies below the water table (§2.6's gate values); each run the table names, and the tunnel run of II.7.3's frontage and lifecycle rules, is one Tunnel record

The condition is this reading of existence and closure, never a second stored state (J-A11.21): it changes only by these conversions — a hand change of a tunnel's condition is the matching convert event (§7.1) — and its open column is what II.7.3's frontage rule and lifecycle read; the same table serves the whole layer (items 64, 65): every gallery and chamber of II.7.6's systems and the undercity (II.7.5) takes this ladder, conversions and table (Gallery.closure, Chamber.closure §2.7), the flooded row theirs alone — reached by DeclineOp's flood (§4.11; J-A65.48) — undone by reopen; a chamber closes its plots as a tunnel run closes its frontage plots (II.7.5)

An access point's state follows its element (item 64): it reads collapsed while its element is partly caved in or collapsed and bricked while sealed — derived readings, never stored by the conversion, so a reopen gives back the access's own stored state (open, locked or bricked, II.7.4); a link of the connection graph (II.7.6) reads collapsed or flooded by the same rule

No epoch rule ever demolishes a tunnel: the engine's plan may not contain demolish on a tunnel record (a hook test lints it), while a user's delete stays available (everything is editable, J-A11.41); a closed tunnel persists as an underground ruin — record live at its address, centreline and invert kept, drawn by §8.2's silted, caved-in and sealed classes through the underground layer's cut-away (§8.4) — and later growth reopens it (reopen; regrowth-first: a closed tunnel on the network's line reopened before a new one is dug) or reuses it: AM-12's underground plots front a reopened tunnel as any navigable one; decline follows the surface's drivers and lag: a tunnel's exposure is the exposure of the ground it runs under, its dwell bands two steps slower than a building's (§4.11's table); emulation: no reference has sewers or time; with the network absent nothing runs

Where the rest of the sewer layer is stated (items 12, 14, 64, 65): existence by tier and toggle-as-visibility, the drain connection rule, the network stage's gate, its levels on the underground arena, the tunnel profile (wall thickness, depth, outfalls), the underground neighbourhoods along navigable tunnels and the basement accesses are II.7.1–II.7.4's; the undercity II.7.5's; the other systems, depths, connection graph and pieces an access edit generates II.7.6's; II.6 keeps the islands, the network stage's declaration, its rule families and presets, and the lifecycle of every underground element

II.7 intro — the underground layer as a whole (owner 2026-09-27 quote; item 65): the sewer network is the central piece of one underground layer that also holds catacombs, caverns, quarries and mine voids, cisterns and vaults, a buried old town where history made one, the private passages an access edit digs, and the undercity — each system its own arena part (the sewer part 0; J-A65.31), all drawn and edited as one layer by depth band, joined to one another and the surface by typed links that exist by rule and chance, never by guarantee; II.7.1–II.7.4 the sewer, neighbourhoods, basement accesses; II.7.5 undercity; II.7.6 other systems; all staged: the base carries the rows, fields, interfaces, invariants and tests these subsections name

II.7 plain words: the owner ruled (items 12, 14): a town may or may not have sewers, a city or metropolis always does and its switch only decides whether they are drawn; some sewer systems carry underground neighbourhoods whose plots may only line a sewer tunnel and whose buildings stand flush against its outer wall; there are no sewer alleys; this section states those rules as mechanisms (rung row, feature draw, two stages with declared I/O, rule tables, invariants and tests), so the layer is a registration not a redesign; network stage's declaration, rule families, presets and lifecycle stay in II.6; records §2.7's; nothing built in the base except the rows, fields, invariants and tests named

II.7.1 The rung row (item 14): RungProfile.layers.sewers (§1.1; one row per rung in ladder.json, calibratable, §7.6) states whether the network exists: THORP, HAMLET, VILLAGE (village product's rows, PART III) never; TOWN law: P(sewers) = clamp(base + populationWeight·(population − 1 500) ÷ 8 500 + wealthWeight·wealthLevel, 0, cap), defaults base 0.05, populationWeight 0.25, wealthWeight 0.30, cap 0.60 (our own values, provenance "architecture 2026-09-26", PLAUSIBLE until calibrated; J-T, §13.7); CITY, METROPOLIS always; population the request's (§1.1), wealthLevel the intent's town-wide wealth control in [0, 1] (§7.7; default 0.5); probability rises with both, never reaches 1 inside the band (cap): a large rich town three times in five, a small poor one once in twenty

The draw (J-A14.41): one of S0's auto features (§4.2 S0): Blueprint.toggles.sewers ∈ {auto, on, off}; a TOWN's auto resolved by this law from blueprint.features before any other stage, recorded in autoResolved with reason (§5.4); on and off honoured as requested; at CITY and METROPOLIS the row fixes existence on whatever the request says: a requested off honoured as a hidden layer and reported in requestedVsBuilt ("network built, layer hidden")

Features.sewers: boolean is a derived field of the document, recomputed on every replay from seed and request (§2.9), listed in the report; every dependant — network stage, drain rule, underground pseudo-district, exporters — reads it from the model, never the view; until the two staged stages are built Features.sewers is resolved and reported and the sewer's arena (part 0) stays empty: the layer's requested row reads omitted with cause staged (§5.1 (7)), so a CITY never claims a network it does not carry

The toggle is visibility (J-A14.42): the app's one Sewers control (§7.8's registry) has two meanings by rung declared in its registry row: at TOWN the model feature (auto/on/off; continuity class discrete; locality class re-derive from the network stage — II.7.2 and II.7.3 run again on part 0 and the ground stays byte-identical, §7.3); at CITY and METROPOLIS a view control that sets the underground LayerSpec.visible through setLayer (§7.1, §8.4) and changes no model; visible false by default at every rung (D-3; MFCG and FTG draw no sewers); the network exists in the model at CITY and METROPOLIS whether or not drawn: §8.4's cut-away or overlay shows it when asked, §11's exporters write the underground layer when its exportSeparately says so; the drain rule and underground neighbourhoods depend on the model, not the view

Which plot rules depend on the network (J-A14.44) — exactly two: (1) the drain rule: the class table's drain column (none, pit, channel) names each class's need; the network stage connects plots to tunnels by the connection table and records each connection on the tunnel (Tunnel.serves, §2.7) — a one-way cross-arena link by entity id (§2.2 rule 2), read back through a resolved view drainOf(plot) (J-K3), so no ground record changes; an unconnected plot drains to its own pit or the street gutter and draws nothing (no cess-pit geometry, no pin); without a network (a TOWN whose draw came out off, every village) the rule does nothing: channel classes keep the requires 'water' gate (§10.2) and S10b's downstream and downwind scoring (§4.7); (2) the underground neighbourhoods (II.7.3), which exist only along navigable tunnels; S10b's siting, S11's site plans and S12b's greenery read nothing else from the network (emulation-first, item 23)

Connection table (defaults, calibratable): historical preset — channel plots connected when a main lies within reachM = 60 m of its frontage midpoint, else reported as unconnected; pit plots connected by a per-band share drawn from the plot's sewer stream: poor 0, modest 0.10, prosperous 0.30, rich 0.60; navigable preset — channel reachM = 120 m; pit every band 1.0 within reachM

II.7.2 The network stage: the declaration is II.6's (SewerStrategy, after S11; families; presets; the lifecycle of item 11); the gate: declared inputs Features.sewers, the ways with flowToward (§2.4), Terrain.hydro and outfalls (§2.3), plots and buildings with the drain column, the underground arena; outputs Tunnel records (under.tunnels); runs only when Features.sewers is true, otherwise commits nothing and part 0 stays schema-complete and empty (§2.1); every other part is II.7.6's; runs eagerly on the generation worker after the derivation pool's merge (reads every district's committed L3 and L4, §4.1); names its tunnels with S13a's naming engine as the underground stage names its own (II.7.3); S14's display list and §11's exporters read the model through the entity registry (§4.10, §8.1) after every registered stage, so tunnels are drawn and exported with no change to S14

The underground arena's levels (J-A12.31, J-A12.32; level mapping §2.2 rule 1): the stage writes on the sewer's part 0 (J-A65.31) in §3.3's one-level batches: L0 one land face, the rock, bounded by the arena's outer ring (the ground's frame plus context margin, §3.2 (9)), written before any tunnel as S1 writes the ground's ring; L1 every tunnel's centreline as a tunnel chain, never a way (no alley, lane or street underground: rule U2); L2 corridorUnion on the L1 faces (§3.7): each tunnel's band (bore plus a wall each side) as two half-corridor strips with junction wedges, and the rock between the bands as the underground's built blocks; the band's outer ring is the tunnel's external wall, the kerb every underground plot line ends on (§3.7); L3 and L4 the underground stage's (II.7.3); nothing writes the ground: the outfall is an entity link (Tunnel.outfall), served plots ids (serves), the street a main follows is follows (§2.7)

Tunnel profile (rule table keyed by (kind, preset); kernel reads a tunnel's corridor half-width as widthCm ÷ 2 + wallCm, §3.7): drain either preset bore 40, headroom 60, wall 25, navigable never; culvert historical/navigable 80/120, 120/180, 40/50, no/yes; main historical 100·(servedHa ÷ 10)^0.3 in [100, 180], 150·(servedHa ÷ 10)^0.2 in [150, 210], 50, navigable where bore and headroom both reach the thresholds (a large trunk main in a big city, rarely a whole system); main navigable 240, 260, 60, always; passage navigable only 150, 220, 50, always

navigable derived per tunnel — widthCm ≥ 110 ∧ headroomCm ≥ 160 (thresholds table values) — and stored on the record (Tunnel.navigable, Tunnel.headroomCm, §2.7); it is what item 12 (b) means by a navigable tunnel, so historical has few or no underground quarters and navigable can have many (J-A14.43); navigable preset is D-3's fantasy toggle, off by default; historical is realism and the network every CITY and METROPOLIS carries

Depth and fall: a tunnel's invert profile (§2.7; invert_knot on the centreline) laid from the head of its run to the outfall: at every knot invert = groundHeightAt(p) − coverCm − headroomCm, lowered where needed so the profile falls monotonically toward the outfall at no less than minGradient (1 : 200) — the monotone-bed rule of the river's carve (§4.2 S1 (3)) — coverCm (crown's depth under the street: 150) a table value; a run needing more fall than the ground gives is re-routed toward the nearer outfall by the family's rule, never trenched (the stage's ladder row, §5.2); elevationCm (§2.1's layer field) on every tunnel is its invert's mean, negative below the ground datum; outfalls are §2.3's outfalls on the settlement's downstream side (ContextVector.upstream ≥ 0.5 at the outfall's cell) — downstream of the harbour and of every water mill's intake (a policy row)

Tunnel editing: a tunnel is an edit target like a way (§7.1 edit-target table: draw, move, delete, setAttr on its kind, bore and headroom; its condition changes only through silt, caveIn, seal, reopen conversions, a hand change of the condition being the matching convert; the preset is the network's): in the base a user may cut, move, seal, reopen or delete any tunnel; the evolution engine never demolishes one (item 11, II.6); every tunnel edit re-derives the underground blocks the edited edges bound (II.7.3's scoping) and nothing on the ground

The owner's rules as hard invariants (§5.3 check rows the determinism part's): U1–U3 are the sewer network's rules, holding on its arena (part 0; J-A65.42) — "there are no sewer alleys" stays true in the sewer — while the undercity (II.7.5) and other systems (II.7.6) are other parts with rules of their own

U1 — frontage on one tunnel, doors onto it: every underground plot's frontage rows lie on the kerb (external wall) of exactly one navigable, open tunnel run, and its access rows are a subset of its frontage rows (§2.5): a door opens only onto the tunnel

U2 — no sewer alleys: the underground L1 carries tunnel chains only; no way chain, no alley face, no S8 lane underground, so no tunnel exists to give access alone; F-PLOT's alley rung is skipped on the underground arena (§5.2): a plot that cannot front a tunnel is not a plot but residue

U3 — flush against the outer wall: every underground building's frontage side lies on its plot's frontage edge; footprint = plot ∩ the frontage band of the row depth (§4.7 S11's boolean), so the room's wall is the tunnel's wall by construction

Who lives there (J-A12.44): the underground is a pseudo-district (District.kind = 'underground', one per settlement, its faces the underground built blocks, its allocation an S7b record), as the hinterland and sky pseudo-districts are; S7b (6) — after the sky pseudo-districts (5), before the districts (1) — creates its Allocation when Features.sewers is on and the preset yields navigable mains (navigable preset always; historical when the trunk law gives at least one navigable run of minRunM = 60 m, predicted at S7b from the arterials' and main roads' served areas, which exist by then since the mains follow them): (a) households of the poorest band, a share undergroundShare of that band's demand (defaults TOWN 0.02, CITY 0.04, METROPOLIS 0.06); (b) classes whose row carries underground 'preferred' (crypts, cold stores, cellar workshops of brewers and vintners, guild vaults) at their table share, plus clandestine institutions whose concealment mode is underground (item 63) — where an undercity exists they go to it first (II.7.5, S7b (7)); where no underground allocation can take them the mode falls back to a front — and any assigned or dossier institution whose knownTo is secret (item 30) for which the assignment templates prefer underground plots; (c) in an epoch, the engine's crowding hook: crowdingShare (II.7.4) of the poorest band's households in the epoch's residual demand (what §4.11's regrowth-first steps (0)–(5) leave) goes underground before the boundary widens (§4.11 (6); J-A12.47), staged with the engine

Underground allocation cap: capped by the predicted capacity — 2 sides × the navigable run length ÷ the poorest band's mean frontage, less the excluded ground — the ground's districts receive the remainder (population whole); a miss between prediction and built network absorbed by S10b's plan–fit–reconcile and F-SITING's ladder, reported, never re-rolled

Prosperity underground is the ground's field shifted: a plot's ContextVector.prosperity = ground raster sampled at the plot's frontage midpoint + undergroundOffset (default −0.25, table value), clamped to [0, 1], banded by the town's own FieldBands (§4.5); density and greenery fields read the same way; ContextVector.arena = 'underground' keys the arena-specific rows

The granularity table (§4.7 S10 (2)) does what the owner asked without a new law: poor band rows many small cells, institution row few large vaults; UndergroundRule (II.7.4) scales their depth by depthScale 0.35 (a plot one or two rooms deep: poor 4–7 m, modest 6–10 m, institution 8–15 m) and sets the vacancy-run share to vacancyRunShare 0.25 (long bare stretches of wall); on the underground arena S11 admits only its arrangements — row and institution (read with ContextVector.arena) — so no compound, detached, hovel, tents or cluster stands along the sewer (the undercity's chambers admit hovels and informal clusters by their own rows, II.7.5; item 70)

The cut is the ground's cut (J-A12.41): on each underground built block the underground stage runs S9's and S10's own machinery with the underground context (PlotStrategy, SitePlanStrategy and BuildingGenerator.outline unchanged, §14): (1) a kerb edge is a frontage when its tunnel is navigable and open (II.6's open column) — drains, culverts and closed runs are not frontages, so a block bounded by drains alone holds only residue; the frontage's class is the tunnel's kind; (2)–(3) as §4.7, claims first for the vaults; (4) per-frontage regions by the straight skeleton, depth capped by the underground depth band, so no plot reaches a second tunnel by construction (two tunnels close together share the medial line between their regions, never a kerb); (5) corner plots at junctions as on the ground; (6) residue typed rock; (7) joins and splits under the same law; (8) vacancy runs at the underground share; (9) no alleys (U2); (10) every plot gets its context vector, derivation record and access rows ⊆ frontage rows (U1); then S10b places the allocation by the same scorer and S11 lays row cells end to end along the wall with party walls, vaults on their claims — the row boolean gives U3

Everything is cut inside the sewer network's arena (part 0): the stage writes only that arena — every transaction keyed to part 0 (§3.4's isolation) — and §13.2's reroll-isolation fixture proves the ground and every other part byte-identical; the ground's static index partitions are read, never touched

The surface constrains the underground — by reads, never copied geometry (J-A12.42, J-A12.43): before a plot is committed its ring is tested on the ground arena through pointLocate and resolve on the ground's PlatKey (§2.2 rule 1, §3.4 services; no cross-arena write, no ground ring copied) at its vertices, its frontage midpoint and a 1 m sample of its rear line; a sample is excluded when it lies in any L0 water face; a cell whose terrainClass is damp or flood (the water table: item 12 (c)); a wall_strip block's band, setback, glacis or ditch part, a tower's or gatehouse's footprint (§4.8); the castle's reservation; the main footprint of a precinct reservation (the cathedral's foundations); and every other L4 footprint — a room under a surface building is that building's own basement (item 29, §2.6), a record of the ground building that never opens onto a tunnel (J-A12.42); public ground (corridors, squares, gate plazas), yard parts, greens, residue and vacant plots allowed

F-UNDER ladder (its §5.2 row is the determinism part's; the rungs are these): an excluded sample steps the plot down: the band's depth → the band's lower depth → the class minimum depth → the run typed vacant (a bare stretch of wall); deterministic from the plot's stream, each use counted in the report; a rear line stopping a metre short of the house above is invisible underground, which is why the test is a sample and not a boolean against ground rings (J-A12.43)

Access, air and light (item 12 (d)): an AccessPoint (II.7.4; in §2.7's entity registry) links the arenas by entity ids — kind (stair, shaft, well, cellar_stair, grating), role (access, air, light), a ground point with the host it opens in (corridor, square, yard or building, resolved on the ground by pointLocate, never a ground face slot) and a vertex on the tunnel's kerb — placed after the plots: every underground neighbourhood (a connected component of open navigable tunnel edges carrying at least one plot) gets at least one access point at the nearest allowed ground point above its tunnels in a declared order: a street stair in a corridor strip or a square; a well shaft in a yard or square; a cellar_stair in a surface building whose basement lies within accessReachM of the neighbourhood's tunnels — the one on a knownTo 'secret' plot (item 30) first, else the one whose class row has the highest access probability at its band (§10.2 undergroundAccess.prob), ties by address (J-A64.44) — a stair from a basement that stays the building's own room (item 29; J-A12.42)

Air and light shafts (grating) placed every shaftSpacingM of navigable tunnel carrying plots (60 m historical, 40 m navigable) on public ground only; where none lies within reach the spacing doubles once, then the run has none, reported; AccessPoint.ground.at moves with its host face under a warp as a pin's point does (§7.4); every grating, well shaft and street stair — every access breaking the surface — is a light shaft for §8.4's lighting, a secret one lit only for a key under which it draws (§8.1 item 7): a column of daylight by day, faint moonlight by night on the floor below (item 68 (d′))

The sewer's light rows (item 68 (d′)): the underground layer has no global light and near-zero ambient; along the sewer the rows of §4.7's light table (LightRule, arena underground, system sewer) put a light at every sewer-front dwelling's door — windows lit by §8.4's derived window lights — and at the tunnels' junctions and access points only; tunnels between them dark; fuel by the settlement's circumstances

Basement accesses (item 64; owner quote; J-A64.41, J-A64.42): beside the neighbourhood rule a surface building may hold its own way down — decided per building by the connection stage (II.7.6), after the underground plots and the layer's other systems, never because a neighbourhood needs one; (1) the gate: the building has a basement (§2.6, item 29) and its Basement.ring lies within accessReachM (5 m; UndergroundRule.access, II.7.4) in plan of an open navigable tunnel's kerb (part 0), of an underground building's side or rear wall (a sewer dwelling — never its frontage — or an undercity building), or where they exist of an open gallery or chamber of another system (II.7.6) or an undercity walkway (II.7.5); test a read through the kernel's services on each part by key (J-A12.32; no cross-arena write), nearest element first, ties by address; the cellar stays a cellar (J-A12.42): the building gains an access record, never a room of the tunnel

Basement access probability: p = min(accessCap, prob × (1 + ageGain × age) × multiplier × crime) — prob the undergroundAccess.prob of the building's class at the plot's band interpolated along the value (§10.2; the front's class where the building carries a concealed use); age ∈ [0, 1] the plot's growth-stage rank (1 for the first stage, 0 for the last: the old houses; ageGain 1); multiplier the concealed class's accessMultiplier where the building carries a concealed use (item 63; default 6), else 1; crime §4.6's access factor 1 + crime.accessScale × PortRows.crime (item 88; 1 while the row is empty); accessCap 0.9; one draw on sewer keyed by the building's lineage (§6.1; no new concern); a class row of 0 (barracks, courthouse, temple) never draws; a user adds an access to any building by item 66's edit (§7.3 item 9; II.7.6)

Basement access kind: follows the drop from the basement's floor to the element's floor: a door through the basement wall where the element is an underground building's wall and the drop within doorDropCm (60); a stair within stairDropCm (300); a ladder beyond; a hatch (the basement plan's trapdoor over a ladder) instead of a stair or ladder where the building carries a concealed use or its basement's own access is a trapdoor

Basement access state and knowledge: state open, locked or bricked by the row's weights (0.6/0.3/0.1 — a bricked-up door the trace of an old one) or an edit, reading collapsed or bricked while its element is closed (II.6); knownTo secret where the building carries a concealed use (item 63) or its plot is knownTo 'secret' (item 30), else local — the one statement of an access's knowledge in a building, which II.7.4 and II.7.6 cite — a brewery's cellar door to the sewer is known to its street

Basement access uses: the access is a fixed anchor of the basement storey that the plan rung reserves — a stair, ladder, trapdoor or door in the basement plan (§2.6, item 28) — and a node of the connection graph (II.7.6): a lifeline where its element is the undercity's (II.7.5); the neighbourhood rule keeps its cellar-stair case as the fallback for a neighbourhood no basement access reaches

Basement access proofs: §5.3's rows (no access without a basement and a reachable element; a concealed building's access secret) and §13.2's T64 bars (the access rate by class within its row; a clandestine building over a network at least at its row's rate)

Depth and ceiling on their own level (item 12 (g); J-A12.45): every underground building's Heights (§2.6) populated as on the ground: baseCm = the tunnel's invert at the plot's frontage midpoint + floorAboveInvertCm (30, above the flow); floors = 1, or 2 for a vault class in the navigable preset where the headroom row allows; eaveCm = the ceiling = min(class storey height, tunnel's headroomCm + vaultAllowanceCm (table: 80 for vaults, 0 for cells)); ridgeCm = eaveCm; roof kind flat (a vault is a style program over the flat kind, §8.2); elevationCm (§2.1) = baseCm, the entity's depth below the ground datum

The sewer network is one arena (PlatKey part 0 of the underground layer, §2.2), not one per depth: depth is per entity inside it (J-A12.45), so tunnels at different depths keep one topology, while the layer's other systems are parts of their own (II.7.6; J-A65.31 amends J-A12.45 for systems); the view groups every part's items into depth bands of depthBandCm (250) for §8.4's cut-away and §11's VTT scenes — one scene per depth band with its elevation

Lifecycle follows the tunnel (item 12 (f)): when a tunnel run's condition closes (II.6's open column false: caved in, collapsed or sealed) every plot whose frontage rows lie on it takes existence abandoned with cause rule:tunnel-closed, its buildings stepping through §2.8's decline states by §4.11's tendency table at the underground's rate; a closed run's plots keep ids, rings and derivation records; reopening (reopen, by the engine or by hand, §7.1) resurrects (§2.8) the plots whose rings still exist, nothing re-rolled; a tunnel deleted by a user takes its plots with it as any way's deletion takes the plots that fronted it (§7.3), and the underground blocks it bounded re-derive

Order, seed and locality (item 12 (h); J-A12.46): UndergroundStrategy registers after the network stage by declared I/O — inputs under.tunnels, the ground plat (read), the three field rasters, the underground Allocation and tables; outputs under.blocks, under.plots, under.buildings, under.access — so city → network → underground plots and buildings; runs eagerly on the generation worker after the pool's merge, never in the pool; keys streams from the underground pseudo-district's lineage through the ordinary concerns (plot.width, plot.join, plot.vacancy, siting, siteplan, heights; the network's own draws use sewer; §6.1); names its entities with S13a's naming engine for its own pseudo-district — a leaf of §9.1's quarter tree in a family of its own, labels drawn only when the layer is visible

Outskirts: the sewer-front blocks on the tunnel runs that lead into an undercity are its outskirts (II.7.5): they keep every rule of this subsection and belong, for naming, description and counts, to the undercity neighbourhood that lists them (District.outskirts, §2.5)

Underground locality: the stage's spatial reads are declared (§7.3's audit): each underground block records the ground cells over it, so an edit whose clear region covers those cells re-derives those blocks by tree scoping onto the dependent arena; a tunnel edit re-derives the blocks its edges bound; a New random of the underground pseudo-district writes only the under arena (part 0) — ground and every other part byte-identical (reroll-isolation fixture §13.2); underground plots and buildings are ordinary plots and buildings on the under/ arena (§2.1's address prefix), so every edit kind, lock, pin, assignment and label of §7 applies unchanged; tunnels and access points have their own edit-target rows (§7.1); stage 2: the underground pseudo-district opens as II.1's underground close-up

Underground emulation note (item 23): neither MFCG nor FTG has sewers or an underground; the whole layer is our extension, staged, hidden by default; with undergroundShare 0 and the layer hidden a CITY reads exactly as the references' city; village rows carry never (PART III)
interface SewerExistenceRow {existence: never|law|always; law?: {base; populationWeight; wealthWeight; cap}} — RungProfile.layers.sewers (§1.1); II.7.1's law

interface Features {sewers: boolean (resolved at S0 from the request and the rung row; re-derived on replay §2.9; read by every dependant); underground: boolean (items 65, 66: true while any underground system exists — the sewer network, a system of II.7.6, or a dug passage alone (II.7.6's closure pieces); derived from the model on every replay; the underground layer's presence, its exporters and the reader read it, never a view)}

interface TunnelProfileRow {kind: Tunnel['kind']; preset: historical|navigable; widthCm: Cm | {base; exp; band: [Cm, Cm]}; headroomCm: Cm | {base; exp; band}; wallCm; coverCm; minGradient; navigableMinWidthCm; navigableMinHeadroomCm} — II.7.2's table; kernel reads widthCm ÷ 2 + wallCm as the corridor half-width (§3.7)

interface AccessPoint {id; kind: stair|ladder|hatch|door|shaft|well|cellar_stair|grating|mouth (ladder, hatch, door: item 64's basement accesses; mouth: an opening in outside ground — a cave mouth, a dug passage's outlet, II.7.6); role: access|air|light; ground: {at: PointCm (moves with its host face under a warp, §7.4); host: Id (corridor, square, yard, building — for a basement access its basement — or outside face)}; under: {part (underground part reached; 0 the sewer); element (tunnel, gallery, chamber or underground building); at: VertexRef (('access_point', id) on the element's kerb or wall, §2.2 rule 7)}; state: open|locked|bricked (item 64 (c): stored; reads collapsed or bricked while its element is closed, derived, never stored); knownTo: public|local|secret (public for a stair, shaft or grating on public ground, local in a yard, in a building by II.7.3 Basement accesses (4) — secret too where an undercity lifeline's row makes it so, II.7.5); source: neighbourhood|basement|system|lifeline|edit; lifecycle: Lifecycle} — §2.8's entity registry

interface UndergroundRule {undergroundShare: Record<Rung, number>; crowdingShare (II.7.3 (c): default 0.10, own, calibratable with the staged engine); undergroundOffset; depthScale; vacancyRunShare; minRunM; floorAboveInvertCm; vaultAllowanceCm; depthBandCm; arrangements: DesignationTemplateRow['arrangement'][] (default ['row', 'institution']); access: {reachM 5; ageGain 1; cap 0.9; doorDropCm 60; stairDropCm 300; state {open 0.6; locked 0.3; bricked 0.1}} (item 64; own values, extension); shaftSpacingM: Record<historical|navigable, number>; excluded: (water|damp|flood|wall_strip|tower|gatehouse|castle|precinct_main|footprint)[]; connection: {reachM: Record<historical|navigable, number>; pitShareByBand: Record<historical|navigable, Record<string, number>>}} — II.7.1's and II.7.3's tables as one editable rule record (§7.6)
